attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Every risk rated high or critical in the risk register has at least one mapped control in the risk-to-control mapping. Zero high/critical risks without a control. FAIL: Any high or critical risk has no mapped control.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The one risk rated 'Elevated' in the register (the entity's top severity label, above 'Moderate' and 'Low') has a mapped control; the register simply doesn't use the literal words 'high' or 'critical' as labels.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: judge the entity's own top-severity tier against the attribute's intent rather than requiring the exact words 'high' or 'critical.' The highest-rated risk here has a control mapped, satisfying the requirement.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The risk-to-control mapping matrix has a control reference filled in on every one of its 14 rows. The risk register it draws from carries 17 risks, of which 5 are rated high; two of those high risks, added at the March review, do not appear in the matrix at all.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Coverage is measured against the population of risks, not against the rows of the mapping document. A matrix in which every listed risk has a control still fails this attribute when high-rated risks from the register never made it into the matrix, because the criterion counts high or critical risks with no mapped control, and here there are two.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show that each significant risk is addressed by at least one control?

attributes.text: General IT controls are implemented across logical access, system operations, and change management
attributes.typical_evidence: IT general controls documentation or control matrix covering access, operations, and change management
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: IT general controls are documented covering all 3 domains: logical access, system operations, and change management. FAIL: IT general controls documentation is missing any of the 3 domains.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: ITGC documentation has clearly labeled sections for 'Logical Access' and 'Change Management,' and system-operations controls (monitoring, backup, incident handling) appear under a section titled 'Infrastructure Operations.'
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: the attribute requires the three control domains to be covered, not that a section be titled exactly 'system operations.' Content under an equivalent heading satisfies the requirement.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show that general it controls are implemented across logical access, system operations?
Does the evidence show that change management?

attributes.text: The entity documents which business processes depend on technology controls
attributes.typical_evidence: Control matrix or documentation showing which business processes depend on which technology components (e.g., access reviews depend on IdP, change management depends on version control)
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Document (control matrix or architecture document) maps at least the key business process-to-technology dependencies (e.g., 'access reviews depend on Okta', 'change management depends on GitHub'). FAIL: No documentation of business process dependencies on technology.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An architecture document contains a narrative paragraph explaining that access reviews depend on the identity provider and that the deploy pipeline depends on the source-control platform, rather than presenting this as a formatted dependency table.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: the attribute asks whether key business-process-to-technology dependencies are documented, not that they appear in table form. A clear narrative description of the same dependencies satisfies the requirement.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show that the entity documents which business processes depend on technology controls?

attributes.text: All users are uniquely identified (no shared accounts for interactive use)
attributes.typical_evidence: User list export from identity provider showing individual accounts
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: User list output from identity provider shows all interactive accounts are individually assigned, no shared/generic accounts (e.g., 'admin', 'devteam', 'shared@'). FAIL: Any shared or generic interactive account is present in production systems. FLAG: Service accounts with interactive login capability that are shared, flag for CPA review.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Identity provider user-list export screenshot shows all 12 employees with individually named accounts (first.last@company.com); no column explicitly labeled 'shared: no'.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Judge what the evidence shows, not how it is labeled. A live system export listing only individually named accounts plainly demonstrates no shared or generic logins exist, even without an explicit 'unique' field itemized.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A client-typed onboarding spreadsheet includes a note 'all user accounts are unique, no shared logins' but no identity provider export or screenshot is attached.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof. This is a config claim about live accounts and needs an actual identity provider export or screenshot, not a self-reported assertion.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that all users are uniquely identified (no shared accounts for interactive use)?

attributes.text: Authentication is required before system access is granted
attributes.typical_evidence: Login page screenshots, SSO configuration, or authentication policy settings
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: System configuration or login page evidence shows every in-scope system requires authentication before granting access. FAIL: Any in-scope system allows unauthenticated access to protected resources.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Screenshot of the production application's login page shows email and password fields required before the dashboard loads; the screenshot does not also show an MFA prompt.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Never import a neighbor attribute's requirement into this one. This attribute only requires that authentication is required before access is granted; MFA strength is tested separately under the MFA control, so its absence from this screenshot is not a failure here.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: During a walkthrough call, the founder states 'our app always requires login, there's no way to skip it' but no screenshot or configuration export is provided.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. A claim about system behavior needs a captured screenshot or config export showing the actual login enforcement, not a spoken assurance.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that authentication is required before system access is granted?

attributes.text: Authentication strength is tiered by system sensitivity
attributes.typical_evidence: Authentication policy or IdP configuration showing strength requirements by system tier
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: System configuration shows production and critical systems require MFA, while non-critical systems require at minimum strong password or SSO. Authentication strength increases with system sensitivity. FAIL: Production or critical systems have weaker authentication than non-critical systems, or all systems have the same minimum authentication regardless of sensitivity.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A two-person company's identity provider policy enforces MFA uniformly across all systems, production and non-production alike, with no separate lower-tier policy defined.
calibration_examples.reasoning: The 'same minimum regardless of sensitivity' fail condition targets a uniformly WEAK floor that leaves a sensitive system underprotected, not a uniformly STRONG one. Applying MFA everywhere is the strongest bar applied universally, so no higher-sensitivity system is weaker than a lower one and the control's intent is fully met.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An internal architecture diagram document states 'production requires MFA, staging requires password only,' but no identity provider configuration screenshot or export corroborates the claim.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A client-authored document is not system proof. A claim about authentication configuration by system tier requires an actual configuration export or screenshot, not a diagram description.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that authentication strength is tiered by system sensitivity?

attributes.text: Standalone or local accounts are minimized and documented
attributes.typical_evidence: List of accounts not managed through the identity provider, with justification
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: All standalone or local accounts not managed through the identity provider are listed with business justification. Zero undocumented standalone accounts. FAIL: Any standalone account has no documented justification, or undocumented standalone accounts are discovered. FLAG: Standalone accounts are documented but justification is generic (e.g., 'convenience', 'legacy'), flag for CPA review.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A standalone break-glass AWS root account is documented in the security register with justification: emergency-use only, MFA-protected, credentials in a sealed vault, access reviewed quarterly.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Compensating controls and documented justification are a legitimate pass path, not a demand that the standalone account be eliminated. A real, verifiable, documented basis for the account (restricted use, MFA, periodic review) satisfies the requirement.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The IT admin states in a call that 'we don't have any standalone or local accounts outside the identity provider' but no actual account inventory or list is produced as evidence.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. Even a claim of zero standalone accounts needs an affirmative, produced list (even an empty one) to substantiate the assertion.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a list of standalone or local accounts not managed through the identity provider?
Is each standalone account documented with business justification?

attributes.text: MFA coverage includes all in-scope production systems, cloud consoles, code repositories, and critical applications
attributes.typical_evidence: MFA policy assignments per application in identity provider showing 'required' for all in-scope systems
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Identity provider configuration shows MFA policy set to 'required' (not 'optional') for all in-scope production systems, cloud consoles, code repositories, and critical applications. 100% coverage, no exceptions without documented risk acceptance. FAIL: MFA policy is set to 'optional' for any in-scope system, or any in-scope system is excluded from MFA enforcement.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show MFA applied to in-scope production systems?
Does the evidence show MFA applied to cloud consoles (AWS, GCP, Azure)?
Does the evidence show MFA applied to code repositories (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket)?
Does the evidence show MFA applied to other critical applications named in scope?

attributes.text: MFA is required for remote or VPN access
attributes.typical_evidence: VPN or remote access configuration showing MFA requirement
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: VPN or remote access configuration shows MFA is required, OR entity has no VPN/remote access capability (pass by default). FAIL: Remote access is available but does not require MFA.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The company is fully cloud-SaaS with no VPN or remote network access layer at all; there is no VPN configuration screenshot in the evidence set.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Structural absence of the underlying capability is a pass path stated directly in the criteria, not a missing artifact. No VPN/remote access capability means the attribute passes by default rather than failing for lack of a VPN screenshot.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A network architecture document lists 'VPN access requires MFA' as a bullet point, but no actual VPN provider configuration export or screenshot is attached.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A client-authored document is not system proof. A configuration claim about MFA enforcement on remote access needs a captured export or screenshot from the VPN or remote-access provider itself.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence confirm whether the entity uses remote access or VPN?
If remote/VPN access exists, does the configuration show MFA required for it?

attributes.text: For each user: MFA is enrolled and active
attributes.typical_evidence: Identity provider user list showing MFA enrollment status for all users
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if identity provider output shows all users have MFA status enrolled and active, with zero users in a not enrolled, inactive, or pending state as of the review date. FAIL if MFA is not enforced or users show no active MFA enrollment. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every user shows MFA enrolled and active throughout the period; an isolated user briefly pending enrollment in an otherwise enforced program is an exception, not a gap; systematic absence of MFA across users is a gap.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include the user list with MFA status?
Does the evidence show MFA enrollment status per user?
Does the evidence show whether MFA is active (not just enrolled) per user?

attributes.text: Documented provisioning process exists
attributes.typical_evidence: Access provisioning procedure or onboarding checklist with access steps
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Procedure document or onboarding checklist describes provisioning steps covering new hires, role changes, and contractors. FAIL: No written provisioning process, or process covers new hires but excludes role changes or contractors.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The onboarding checklist document details provisioning steps for new hires and role changes, and states 'the same process applies to all personnel, including contractors,' without a separate contractor-specific section.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: a live document substantively covering contractors through general personnel language passes even without a separately itemized contractor section.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a access provisioning procedure or onboarding checklist with access steps?

attributes.text: Policy requires authorization before access is granted
attributes.typical_evidence: Access management policy stating approval is required before provisioning
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Access management policy document text explicitly states that authorization (approval) must be obtained before access is provisioned. FAIL: Policy does not require pre-provisioning authorization, or allows access to be granted before approval.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The access management policy states 'manager sign-off is required before any account is created' rather than using the literal word 'authorization.'
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: substantively equivalent language requiring pre-provisioning approval satisfies the attribute even without the exact word 'authorization.'

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a relevant policy document?
Does the policy require authorization before access is granted?

attributes.text: For each provisioning event: access request and approval are documented
attributes.typical_evidence: Ticketing system records, email approvals, or HRIS workflow showing access request and approval
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if the most recent provisioning event has a documented access request and a documented approval, both with timestamps, and approval occurred before or on the same day access was granted. FAIL if the provisioning process produces no request records or no approval records at all. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every provisioning event in the period has a timestamped request and a timestamped approval with approval on or before the grant date; an isolated event with a missing timestamp in an otherwise documented practice is an exception, not a gap; systematic absence of requests or approvals, or access routinely granted before approval, is a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The most recent new-hire ticket contains a request comment from HR and a timestamped reply from the manager reading 'approved, please provision,' both inside the same ticket thread rather than as separate record types.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: a timestamped approval comment within the same ticket thread is a legitimate documented approval, and the attribute does not require request and approval to live in separate record types.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual ticketing system records (not just a verbal description)?
Does the record show that access request?
Does the record show that approval are documented?

attributes.text: For each provisioning event: approval is from an authorized approver (manager or system owner)
attributes.typical_evidence: Approval records showing approver identity and their authorization to approve
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if the most recent provisioning event shows approval from a manager or system owner who is a different person than the requester, with no self approval. FAIL if the process permits self approval or defines no authorized approver role. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every provisioning event in the period shows approval by a manager or system owner distinct from the requester; an isolated event routed to a valid alternate approver is an exception, not a gap; systematic self approval, or approval by someone who is not a manager or system owner, is a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A provisioning ticket for AWS console access lists the same username in both the requester field and the approver field.
calibration_examples.reasoning: An approval step existing is not the same as an authorized approval. The criteria require approval from a manager or system owner distinct from the requester, and a matching requester and approver identity is self-approval, which is a gap regardless of the presence of an approval field.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Solo founder with one contractor. The only provisioning event in the period is the contractor's repository and staging access: the contractor requested it in a message thread, the founder approved it in the same thread before granting it, and the procedure names the founder as the approver for every grant to another person.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Requester and approver are different people here, so the event passes on its own terms. A one-person company's procedure names the founder as the authorized approver for any access granted to someone else, which is a defined approver role; the founder's own owner accounts exist because the founder created the systems and are inventoried under privileged access, not requested and approved as provisioning events.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual approval records showing approver identity and their authorization to approve (not just a verbal description)?
Does the record show that approval is from an authorized approver (manager or system owner)?

attributes.text: For each provisioning event: access granted matches the authorized request
attributes.typical_evidence: Comparison of approved access request against actual access provisioned in the system
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if the most recent provisioning event shows the access actually granted matches the access specified in the approved request, with no additional roles, permissions, or systems beyond what was requested. FAIL if access is granted with no reference to an approved scope. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every provisioning event in the period shows granted access matching the approved request; an isolated minor discrepancy later corrected in an otherwise controlled practice is an exception, not a gap; systematic granting of access beyond what was approved is a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The access comparison record shows the new hire received the requested engineering role plus a standard company-wide read-only baseline group that is automatically applied to every employee account.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: an automatically applied, organization-wide baseline group is not additional access beyond the request in substance, and should not be treated as scope creep just because it was not separately itemized in the request.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The approved access request for a new support hire specifies the helpdesk tool and read-only access to the booking console. The identity provider export for that user shows both of those, plus membership in the 'billing-admin' group granted the same afternoon. No request or approval mentions billing.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Matching runs in both directions, so access present in the system but absent from the approved request fails this attribute just as squarely as access that was requested and never granted. The criteria call out additional roles beyond what was requested, and an unrequested admin group is the case they exist for.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual comparison of approved access request against actual access provisioned in the system (not just a verbal description)?
Does the record show that access granted matches the authorized request?

attributes.text: Documented offboarding/deprovisioning process exists
attributes.typical_evidence: Offboarding procedure or checklist covering access revocation steps
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Offboarding procedure or checklist document lists access revocation steps for all in-scope systems. FAIL: No documented offboarding process, or process does not cover all in-scope systems.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The offboarding checklist instructs staff to 'revoke all system access per the current access inventory' rather than naming each of the company's 15 in-scope systems individually.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: referencing the maintained access inventory as the authoritative source for revocation substantively covers all in-scope systems without re-listing each one in the checklist itself.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a offboarding procedure or checklist covering access revocation steps?

attributes.text: Policy defines maximum timeframe for access removal upon termination
attributes.typical_evidence: Access management or offboarding policy specifying access removal timeline (e.g., same day, within 24 hours)
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Policy document text states a specific maximum timeframe for access removal (e.g., 'same day', 'within 24 hours', 'within 1 business day'). FAIL: Policy uses vague language ('promptly', 'as soon as possible') without a defined timeframe, or does not address access removal timing.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The offboarding policy states access must be removed 'by end of business day on the termination date' rather than using the phrase '24 hours.'
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: 'end of business day' is a specific, defined maximum timeframe that satisfies the requirement just as well as an hour-count phrasing.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show that policy defines maximum timeframe for access removal upon termination?

attributes.text: For each termination: access removed within the defined timeframe
attributes.typical_evidence: IdP disable date compared to HR termination date for each terminated individual
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if the most recent termination shows the identity provider account disabled or deleted within the policy defined timeframe of the human resources termination date, measured as the disable timestamp minus the termination date; if no policy window is defined, within 5 business days. FAIL if terminated individuals are not deprovisioned at all or no timeframe governs removal. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every termination in the period shows access revoked within the defined timeframe; an isolated termination revoked slightly outside the window in an otherwise timely practice is an exception, not a gap; systematic revocation outside the timeframe is a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The company's offboarding policy defines a 3-business-day removal window; the most recent termination shows the identity provider account disabled 2 business days after the HR termination date.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Judge against the entity's own documented timeframe, not an assumed industry norm such as same-day removal. Removal within the client's defined 3-business-day window satisfies the attribute even though it is not instantaneous.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A one-person company's offboarding procedure sets a same-day removal window. Nobody has been employed and left since founding; the one departure is a contractor whose repository and staging access was removed the day the engagement ended, shown by the repository's own access log.
calibration_examples.reasoning: The population is every person whose access ended, and here that is one contractor, removed inside the stated window with the system's own log as proof, which passes. A solo founder who has not left their own company is not a termination, and zero employee terminations is zero events rather than a gap.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual idp disable date compared to hr termination date for each terminated individual (not just a verbal description)?
Does the record show that access removed within the defined timeframe?

attributes.text: For each termination: all in-scope system access is removed
attributes.typical_evidence: Access verification across all in-scope systems for each terminated individual
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if the most recent terminated individual has zero active accounts across all in scope systems, including the identity provider, cloud consoles, code repositories, and business applications. FAIL if terminated individuals retain active access with no removal process. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every terminated individual has no active accounts remaining on any in scope system; an isolated lingering account on a single system in an otherwise complete practice is an exception, not a gap; systematic retention of access after termination is a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The termination verification record confirms the identity provider account was disabled, but no check is documented for the same individual's cloud console, code repository, or business application access.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Partial-system evidence should not be credited as complete coverage. The criteria require zero active accounts across all in-scope systems, and confirming only the identity provider leaves cloud consoles, code repos, and business apps unverified, which is a gap in coverage, not a pass.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual access verification across all in-scope systems for each terminated individual (not just a verbal description)?
Does the record show that all in-scope system access is removed?

attributes.text: For each termination: offboarding completion is tracked with timestamps
attributes.typical_evidence: Offboarding checklist with timestamps for each deprovisioning step
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if the most recent offboarding record includes timestamps for key deprovisioning steps, at minimum when the identity provider was disabled and when systems access was revoked. FAIL if offboarding is not tracked or records carry no timestamps. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every offboarding record in the period includes timestamps for the deprovisioning steps; an isolated record missing a single timestamp in an otherwise tracked practice is an exception, not a gap; systematic absence of deprovisioning timestamps is a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The offboarding record shows timestamps for identity provider disablement and systems access revocation, but no timestamp for a peripheral checklist line item like laptop return.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: the criteria only require timestamps for the minimum key deprovisioning steps, IdP disable and systems access revocation, both of which are present; a missing timestamp on an unrelated checklist item like equipment return is outside this attribute's scope.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual offboarding checklist with timestamps for each deprovisioning step (not just a verbal description)?
Does the record show that offboarding completion is tracked with timestamps?

attributes.text: Policy requires access reviews by system owners or management
attributes.typical_evidence: Access management policy specifying review requirements, reviewer role, and frequency
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Access management policy document requires periodic access reviews conducted by system owners or management (not end users reviewing their own access) and specifies the review frequency. FAIL: Policy does not require periodic access reviews, or reviews are to be conducted by end users.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The access review requirement appears as a clause inside the company's combined 'Access Control and Onboarding/Offboarding Policy' rather than in a standalone 'Access Review Policy,' stating management reviews access quarterly.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: judge the substance of what the policy requires, not the document title or section heading it lives under. The clause plainly requires periodic reviews by management with a stated quarterly frequency, which is exactly what the attribute tests, so it passes regardless of which policy file contains it.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an access management policy document?
Does the policy require access reviews?
Does the policy specify that reviews are conducted by system owners or management?

attributes.text: Review scope covers all in-scope systems
attributes.typical_evidence: Access review scope documentation or checklist listing all in-scope systems
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Access review scope documentation or checklist lists all in-scope systems, compare against the entity's in-scope system list and confirm no systems are excluded. FAIL: Any in-scope system is excluded from the access review scope.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The access review scope checklist lists 'cloud infrastructure' and 'core SaaS tools' as umbrella categories covering AWS, GCP, and the HR system, rather than naming each system individually.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: a category umbrella that demonstrably includes every in-scope system satisfies the attribute even without itemizing each system by name. Confirm the umbrella actually maps to the full in-scope list before failing on formatting alone.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show what systems are covered by access reviews?
Does the review scope include all systems confirmed in the audit scope?

attributes.text: For each access review: review was performed at least {review_frequency}
attributes.typical_evidence: Access review records with dates showing reviews occurred at the defined frequency
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if the entity has a defined access review frequency and the most recent review was performed on schedule, with dated records showing the review occurred. FAIL if no review has been performed or no review frequency is defined. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if dated access review records show a review in every required period at the entity's defined frequency, for example four reviews in a 12 month period where the frequency is quarterly; an isolated review completed slightly late in an otherwise consistent cadence is an exception, not a gap; a required review period with no review record at all is a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The most recent access review is logged as a dated, completed task in the team's shared Notion tracker rather than in a dedicated access-review tool, showing the review was performed on the quarterly schedule.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Process-exists attributes pass on the existence and timing of the review, not the hygiene or format of the tool used to log it. A dated record in an ordinary task tracker is still a dated record if it shows the review occurred on schedule.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include dated records of actual reviews performed?
Do the review dates match the frequency the policy specifies?

attributes.text: For each review: review covers all in-scope systems
attributes.typical_evidence: Access review records listing systems reviewed, compared against in-scope system list
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if the most recent review record lists the systems reviewed and all in scope systems appear in that review. FAIL if reviews do not enumerate systems or omit in scope systems entirely. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every review record in the period lists the systems reviewed with every in scope system covered; an isolated review missing one recently added system in an otherwise complete practice is an exception, not a gap; systematic exclusion of an in scope system is a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The reviewer states in an interview note that 'all systems were checked' during the last access review, but the review record itself only lists AWS and GitHub with no mention of the company's newly adopted Slack workspace.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never a substitute for the review record itself. The written record must enumerate the systems reviewed, and an in-scope system absent from that record is a real coverage gap even if someone claims otherwise verbally.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual review record?
Does the review record show which systems were reviewed?
Are all in-scope systems listed in each review?

attributes.text: For each review: reviewer is the system owner or designated authority
attributes.typical_evidence: Access review records showing reviewer name/role, compared to system owner assignments
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if the most recent review record shows the reviewer is the system owner or designated authority confirmed against the system owner list, and the reviewer is not reviewing their own access. FAIL if reviews are performed by end users over their own access or no reviewer authority is defined. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every review in the period was performed by the system owner or designated authority with no self review; an isolated review delegated to a valid alternate authority is an exception, not a gap; systematic self review, or review by someone who is not the system owner or designated authority, is a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The review record lists the reviewer as 'Admin User' for the production database review, and the AI treats any account with 'Admin' in its name as evidence the system owner performed the review.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Never accept a generic account label at face value without confirming it maps to the actual named system owner. A shared or generic admin account name is not proof that the designated owner performed the review versus a delegate or the account holder reviewing their own access.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual review record?
Does the review record identify who performed the review?
Is the identified reviewer the system owner or a designated authority?

attributes.text: For each review: identified issues are remediated within defined timeframe
attributes.typical_evidence: Review records showing identified access issues and remediation dates
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if issues identified in the most recent review show remediation, meaning access removed or adjusted, completed within the entity's defined timeframe; if no issues were identified, pass by default. FAIL if identified issues carry no remediation process. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every issue identified across the period's reviews shows remediation completed within the defined timeframe, or no issues were identified; an isolated remediation completed slightly late in an otherwise responsive practice is an exception, not a gap; systematic failure to remediate identified issues, or remediation routinely outside the defined timeframe, is a gap.
attributes.na_condition: Pass if no inappropriate access was identified in the period's reviews

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A flagged over-permissioned account from the last review was removed the same week, evidenced only by a timestamped Slack message from the reviewer confirming the access was revoked, with no formal ticketing system in use.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: a timestamped message confirming remediation is sufficient proof of timely action for a small team without a formal ticketing system. Demanding a specific ticket format when the substance (dated removal within the defined timeframe) is clearly shown is over-literal.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual review record?
Does the record show whether any issues were identified?
For any identified issues, are remediation actions documented?
For any identified issues, does the evidence show remediation within the entity's defined timeframe?

attributes.text: Access roles are defined and documented
attributes.typical_evidence: Role definitions in identity provider or access control matrix showing role permissions
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Identity provider or access control system shows defined roles with documented permissions per role. FAIL: No defined roles, or roles have no documented permissions.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An Okta screenshot shows named groups (Engineering, Finance, Admin) each with a description field listing their associated permissions, but there is no separate written 'role definitions' document.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Live system evidence showing defined roles and their permissions passes even without a companion policy document. The identity provider's own configuration is system evidence of documented roles regardless of whether a redundant document also exists.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A submitted 'Future Access Model' project document lists proposed roles and permissions but is marked 'DRAFT - pending implementation' with several TODO placeholders and no adoption date.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A draft or project document is not an adopted configuration. Placeholder text and an explicit draft banner mean the roles described are not yet in force, so this fails until the roles are shown as actually implemented in the system.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show defined access roles?
Are the roles documented with their associated permissions?

attributes.text: Access is assigned through roles or groups (not individual grants)
attributes.typical_evidence: IdP group assignments or access control configuration showing role-based assignment
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: IdP configuration shows access assigned through roles or groups for the majority of users. Individual grants, if any, are documented with justification. FAIL: Access is primarily assigned through individual grants without role/group structure. FLAG: More than 20% of access grants are individual (not role-based), flag for CPA review.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An Okta export shows the large majority of employees assigned access via groups, with two long-term contractors holding individual app grants that each have a documented business justification note attached.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: the pass criteria explicitly tolerate a minority of individual grants when documented with justification, so a small number of justified exceptions is not a structural failure. Only access primarily assigned through ungoverned individual grants should fail this attribute.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A client-authored spreadsheet states '95% of access is assigned through groups' with no accompanying identity-provider export or screenshot to substantiate the figure.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof for a configuration claim. This attribute tests actual IdP assignment structure, which requires a system export or screenshot corroborating the stated percentage, not a self-reported figure.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A one-person company: the identity provider and each in-scope system show a single human account holding the owner or administrator role, and three service accounts each scoped to a named function; there are no group assignments because there is nobody to group.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Role based assignment at the size of one user is a defined role held by the one account plus function-scoped service accounts, not a group structure with one member. The attribute fails access that is primarily ungoverned individual grants, and an owner role with scoped service accounts is the opposite of that; do not import a fleet expectation onto one person.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that access is assigned through roles or groups (not individual grants)?

attributes.text: For each user: role assignments align with job functions
attributes.typical_evidence: Comparison of users' role assignments against their job titles/functions
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if all users' role assignments match their job title and function, with no admin roles assigned to non admin personnel and no production access for non technical roles. FAIL if roles are assigned with no relationship to job function. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every user has role assignments that align with their job function; an isolated over broad assignment later corrected in an otherwise least privilege practice is an exception, not a gap; systematic misalignment, for example a developer holding billing administration or a human resources user holding production shell access, is a gap. FLAG: role assignment is plausible but the job function description is ambiguous, flag for CPA review.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A DevOps engineer holds both AWS infrastructure-admin access and read-only billing console access; the job description confirms cost-monitoring duties as part of the role.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: an access grant that falls outside the narrowest reading of a job title still aligns with job function when the job description documents the underlying duty. Verify against the actual documented responsibilities before flagging a mismatch.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual comparison of users' role assignments against their job titles/functions (not just a verbal description)?
Does the record show that role assignments align with job functions?

attributes.text: Privileged users are inventoried across all in-scope systems
attributes.typical_evidence: Privileged user list per system (admin roles in AWS IAM, GitHub org owners, database admins)
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: A privileged user list per system (admin roles in cloud IAM, org owners in code repos, database admins) covers all in-scope systems. FAIL: No privileged user inventory, or any in-scope system is missing from the inventory.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A live screenshot of the AWS IAM console listing all admin-role users was submitted under a generic file name and initially tagged as a miscellaneous document rather than as system evidence.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Live system screenshots are system evidence regardless of how they were labeled at submission. Judge the content of the corpus, not the filename or tag it arrived with, before concluding the inventory is missing.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A founder-typed spreadsheet lists the names of people believed to have admin access to AWS and GitHub, with no accompanying console export or API pull from either system.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof for a privileged-user inventory. The claim requires an actual export or live capture from each in-scope system, not a list typed from memory.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that privileged users are inventoried across all in-scope systems?

attributes.text: Each privileged user is authorized and has a documented business need
attributes.typical_evidence: Privileged access justification records or approval tickets
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Each privileged user has a documented authorization record (approval ticket, email, or access request) and a business justification for their privileged access. FAIL: Any privileged user lacks documented authorization or business justification.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A privileged access grant is authorized via a timestamped Slack message from the engineering manager approving admin access for a specific incident-response need, with no formal ticketing system in place.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: an informal but verifiable, timestamped approval record satisfies the authorization requirement for a small team without a ticketing system. The substance is a documented approval carrying a business justification, which is what the attribute tests.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: During the walkthrough interview the IT lead states 'we always approve admin access before granting it,' but no approval record, ticket, or email is provided for any of the privileged users.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never a substitute for documented authorization. Each privileged user needs an actual retrievable authorization artifact, not a general assurance given in conversation.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A solo founder holds the administrator or owner role on every in-scope system. The privileged access inventory names the founder for each system with the justification 'sole operator and account owner', dated and kept with the quarterly access review; no approval ticket exists because there is nobody else to approve.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Authorization for a company of one is a documented record, and the founder's dated written justification for each privileged role is that record. The attribute asks for a documented authorization and a business need per privileged user, which a dated inventory entry naming the role and the reason supplies; an approval ticket from a second person is a form the entity cannot produce and the criterion does not demand.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that each privileged user is authorized?
Does the system configuration show that has a documented business need?

attributes.text: Privileged activities are logged
attributes.typical_evidence: Cloud audit logs or SIEM showing admin activity logging enabled
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: System configuration (CloudTrail, Azure Activity Log, SIEM, or equivalent) shows logging enabled for admin/privileged actions across all in-scope systems. Logs capture who (actor), what (action), and when (timestamp). FAIL: Logging is not enabled for privileged activities on any in-scope system, or logs do not capture all three fields (who, what, when).

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A screenshot shows CloudTrail enabled at the AWS Organizations management account as an org-wide trail, which by design also logs activity in every member account, but no per-member-account screenshot was separately captured.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: an organization-wide trail configured at the management account level demonstrably covers every member account by design, so a live capture proving that structure passes without a redundant per-account screenshot.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The evidence submitted is a page from the cloud provider's public documentation describing that CloudTrail 'can log all account activity,' with no screenshot of this organization's own trail configuration.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A provider's documentation page is not this organization's configuration. The attribute requires proof that logging is actually enabled in this entity's own environment, not a description of the feature's general availability.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that privileged activities are logged?

attributes.text: Service accounts are documented with owner and purpose
attributes.typical_evidence: Service account registry or secrets manager inventory with owner and purpose columns
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Service account registry or secrets manager inventory lists each service account with a designated owner and stated purpose. FAIL: Any service account lacks a documented owner or purpose.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A live export from the secrets manager shows each service account's resource tags populated with 'Owner' and 'Purpose' fields, but there is no separate formal service-account registry document.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Live system evidence showing the required fields passes even without a redundant standalone document. The secrets manager's own tagging is system evidence of ownership and purpose regardless of format.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A founder-typed spreadsheet lists each service account with an owner name and purpose description, with no corresponding export from the secrets manager or cloud console to confirm the accounts or fields exist there.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof for a configuration claim. The owner and purpose fields need to be corroborated by an actual system export, not asserted in a self-made document.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that service accounts are documented with owner?
Does the system configuration show that purpose?

attributes.text: Service account credentials are rotated or have defined expiration
attributes.typical_evidence: Secrets manager rotation configuration or credential expiration policy settings
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Secrets manager or KMS configuration shows automatic rotation enabled, OR manual rotation records show credentials rotated per a defined schedule (at minimum annually). FAIL: No rotation schedule or expiration configured for service account credentials.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A secrets manager screenshot shows automatic rotation configured with a rotation Lambda attached to each service credential, but does not show a completed rotation event log or 'last rotated' timestamp.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: this attribute passes on automatic rotation being enabled in configuration, not on a rotation having already executed, which belongs to operating-effectiveness testing elsewhere. A screenshot of the rotation configuration being enabled is sufficient at the design stage.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: During the interview the founder states 'we rotate all service credentials every quarter,' but no secrets manager configuration screenshot or rotation policy setting was provided.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never config evidence. The rotation schedule or automatic rotation setting must be shown in the actual system configuration or in dated manual rotation records, not asserted verbally.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that service account credentials are rotated or have defined expiration?

attributes.text: For each review period: service account review was performed (separate from user access reviews)
attributes.typical_evidence: Service account review records showing last-used dates and removal of inactive accounts
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Service account review records show a review performed within the last 12 months that checked last-used dates and removed or disabled unused accounts. This is distinct from the user access review; a user access review alone does not satisfy it. FAIL: No service account-specific review performed within the last 12 months, or review did not check last-used dates.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The service account review is recorded as a distinct, separately-labeled tab within the same quarterly access-review spreadsheet, showing last-used dates and two disabled unused accounts.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: 'separate from user access reviews' means functionally distinct in scope and method, not housed in an entirely different document or tool. A clearly delineated section that independently evaluates service accounts by last-used date and disables unused ones satisfies the requirement.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual service account review records showing last-used dates and removal of inactive accounts (not just a verbal description)?
Does the record show that service account review was performed (separate from iam-05 user access reviews)?

attributes.text: Network architecture is documented
attributes.typical_evidence: Network architecture diagram showing environments, segments, and connectivity
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Network architecture diagram or document is on file and dated or reviewed within 24 months, showing environments, segments, and connectivity. FAIL: No network architecture documentation, or documentation is dated more than 24 months ago.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Engineering maintains a living architecture page in the team wiki that diagrams the VPCs, subnets, and data flow between services, reviewed and updated four months ago; there is no separate exported diagram file.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A network architecture document can take any durable form (wiki page, diagram tool, slide) as long as it shows environments, segments, and connectivity and was reviewed within 24 months; don't demand a specific file format. The wiki page is current and complete on substance.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show that network architecture is documented?

attributes.text: Production is isolated from non-production environments
attributes.typical_evidence: Cloud network configuration, account structure, or network segmentation settings
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: System configuration shows production is logically separated from non-production (separate VPCs/accounts, separate clusters, separate database instances, or equivalent isolation). FAIL: Production and non-production share the same environment without separation.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An engineer captured a live screenshot of the cloud console showing separate AWS accounts for production and staging, submitted under a generic filename with no explicit lane tag at upload time.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Live system screenshots are system evidence regardless of how they were labeled at submission; judge what the capture shows, not its filename or tag. A plainly separate account structure between prod and staging satisfies isolation.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The client submitted a spreadsheet they typed themselves listing production and staging VPC IDs, with no accompanying console capture or export.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof for a configuration claim. Without a captured export or corroborating system view, the isolation claim is unverified and should be a gap pending an actual console screenshot or export.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that production is isolated from non-production environments?

attributes.text: Access between network segments follows least-privilege rules
attributes.typical_evidence: Security group rules, firewall rules, or network ACL configuration
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Security group rules, firewall rules, or network ACL output shows traffic between segments restricted to specific ports and protocols, no 'allow all' rules between segments. FAIL: Any 'allow all' rule between network segments, or unrestricted traffic between production and non-production.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A security group export shows explicit allow rules scoped to specific ports between segments (app tier to database on 5432 only), with no allow-all entries anywhere, but no written narrative explains each rule's rationale.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: a live export plainly showing scoped, non-allow-all rules passes even without an accompanying narrative explaining least-privilege intent. The rules themselves demonstrate the control.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An engineer stated on a call that production and staging don't share any open network rules, but no security group or firewall export was provided.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. The segmentation claim needs an actual rules export or screenshot before it can pass.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that access between network segments follows least-privilege rules?

attributes.text: Boundary protection mechanisms are configured
attributes.typical_evidence: WAF configuration, load balancer settings, or firewall rule export
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: System configuration shows at least one boundary protection mechanism (WAF, firewall, security groups, or network ACLs) is configured and in active/enabled state. FAIL: No boundary protection mechanisms configured, or mechanisms are in disabled/bypass state.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A three-person startup runs on a managed hosting platform behind a CDN provider; a screenshot shows the CDN's proxy/WAF toggle enabled on the production domain, with no dedicated firewall appliance in place.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Compensating controls are a legitimate pass path at design stage: a cloud-native boundary mechanism like a managed WAF/proxy satisfies this attribute at this scale. The pass should state explicitly that it rests on the compensating cloud-native control.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The evidence submitted was a screenshot of the CDN provider's public marketing page describing its WAF product, not a screenshot of the client's own zone or domain settings.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A provider's marketing or trust page is not this org's configuration. The entity must show its own dashboard or zone settings with the mechanism actually enabled for its domain.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that boundary protection mechanisms are configured?

attributes.text: Only required ports and protocols are permitted inbound
attributes.typical_evidence: Security group inbound rules or firewall rule export showing allowed ports
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Security group or firewall inbound rules show no 0.0.0.0/0 (unrestricted) access on non-public ports. Only ports required for public services (80, 443) may have unrestricted source. FAIL: Any non-public port (SSH/22, RDP/3389, database ports, admin ports) allows 0.0.0.0/0 inbound access.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A firewall export shows exactly two inbound rules: port 443 open to all, and port 80 redirecting to 443; no other ports appear anywhere in the rule set.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: a fully captured rule set with only public web ports open is itself proof that nothing else is exposed. Don't demand a rule explicitly stating that admin ports are closed when the complete export shows none exist.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The client typed a note stating that SSH access is restricted to the office IP address; no firewall or security group export was attached.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A client-authored note is not system proof. A port-restriction claim needs an actual firewall or security-group export or console screenshot.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that only required ports?
Does the system configuration show that protocols are permitted inbound?

attributes.text: External access points are inventoried
attributes.typical_evidence: List of public-facing endpoints, domains, and IP addresses
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: A list of external access points (public-facing endpoints, domains, IP addresses) is documented and maintained. FAIL: No documented list of external access points.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Engineering maintains an internal wiki page listing every public subdomain and its purpose, last reviewed and updated within the quarter.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Solo/small-team proportionality: a maintained internal list is the proportional artifact for this attribute at this company's size. Existence and currency of the inventory is what's tested, not the specific tool used to produce it.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The hosting provider's public status page, listing the provider's own infrastructure regions, was submitted as the entity's external access point inventory.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A provider's infrastructure page is not this org's configuration. The entity needs its own list of its domains, endpoints, and IP addresses, not the vendor's general infrastructure description.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that external access points are inventoried?

attributes.text: Remote access requires MFA and encrypted connection
attributes.typical_evidence: VPN or remote access configuration showing MFA and encryption requirements
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Remote access configuration shows MFA required AND encrypted connections enforced (TLS 1.2+ or VPN with encryption). FAIL: Remote access lacks MFA or allows unencrypted connections.
attributes.na_condition: N/A if entity has no remote access capability

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The team uses a device-based zero-trust access tool gated by SSO and MFA with encrypted tunnels, instead of a traditional VPN client.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Compensating controls are legitimate at design stage: a zero-trust access tool enforcing MFA and encryption is equivalent to a VPN for this attribute. State the compensating basis explicitly when passing.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The IT admin said on a call that remote access requires MFA, but no VPN or zero-trust configuration screenshot or export was submitted.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. The MFA-and-encryption claim needs an actual configuration capture showing both requirements enforced.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that remote access requires mfa?
Does the system configuration show that encrypted connection?

attributes.text: Physical access to facilities requires authorization before being granted
attributes.typical_evidence: Badge/key card system configuration or physical access request form
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Badge/key card system configuration or access request form shows physical access requires authorization before being granted. FAIL: Physical access is unrestricted or granted without authorization.
attributes.na_condition: N/A if entity has no physical facilities

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The four-person company works out of a shared coworking space with no dedicated leased facility; the coworking operator's badge system gates entry to the building and floor, documented as the client's physical access control.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Solo/small-team proportionality: for a company with no facility of its own, a shared building's badge-gated access is the proportional control. State the compensating basis explicitly when passing.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The office manager said in an interview that a badge is required to enter the building, with no badge system export, access request form, or building management confirmation provided.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never evidence. A physical access authorization claim needs a badge system screenshot/export or an access request form on file.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that physical access to facilities requires authorization before being granted?

attributes.text: Restricted areas (server rooms, network closets) have additional access controls
attributes.typical_evidence: Separate badge reader or lock configuration for restricted areas
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Configuration or documentation shows restricted areas (server rooms, network closets) have additional access controls (separate badge reader, lock, biometric) beyond general facility access. FAIL: Restricted areas use the same access controls as general facility areas.
attributes.na_condition: N/A if entity has no physical facilities

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The office has one shared key-card reader for the floor; the server closet uses a separate physical lock with keys held only by the two engineers, documented in a short internal access note.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Proportional compensating control: a distinct physical lock restricted to a named subset of personnel satisfies additional access controls beyond general facility access, even without a second badge reader.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The facilities lead said restricted areas have extra security without describing what it is, and no documentation or photo of the actual control was provided.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never evidence. The claim needs a description or capture of the actual additional control (lock type, reader, biometric) in place.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that restricted areas (server rooms?
Does the system configuration show that network closets) have additional access controls?

attributes.text: Physical access is removed when no longer required
attributes.typical_evidence: Offboarding checklist showing badge/key return step, or access system deactivation records
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Offboarding checklist or access system records show physical access revoked (badge deactivated, keys returned) when no longer required. FAIL: No evidence of physical access revocation during offboarding, or devices not recovered.
attributes.na_condition: N/A if entity has no physical facilities

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The offboarding checklist has a line item for badge return and access deactivation, and the two departures logged this quarter both show the box checked with a date, though the checklist template itself hasn't been reformatted in over a year.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Process-exists attributes pass on the existence and use of the process, not the hygiene of its paperwork. A used, dated checklist entry evidencing revocation is sufficient even if the template is old.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show that physical access is removed when no longer required?

attributes.text: Visitors are identified and logged
attributes.typical_evidence: Visitor sign-in log or visitor management system records
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Visitor sign-in log or visitor management system records are maintained with visitor name, date, and host. FAIL: No visitor log maintained.
attributes.na_condition: N/A if entity has no physical facilities

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The small office keeps a paper sign-in sheet at the front desk recording visitor name, date, and who they were meeting; it is not a digital visitor-management system.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Proportional form passes: the attribute tests that visitors are identified and logged, not that a specific software system is used. A maintained paper log with name, date, and host satisfies the control.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include visitor sign-in records or a visitor management log?
Are visitors identified in the records (name, date, host)?

attributes.text: Physical access is reviewed at least annually
attributes.typical_evidence: Physical access review record with date and findings
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Physical access review record dated within the last 12 months shows review performed with documented findings and follow-up actions. FAIL: No physical access review within the last 12 months.
attributes.na_condition: N/A if entity has no physical facilities

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Eight months ago the office manager emailed IT confirming who currently holds a badge and flagging two people to remove; the note isn't titled a physical access review and uses no formal template.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Process-exists attributes pass on substance, not on label or template. A dated review of who holds access with documented follow-up action satisfies the annual review requirement even without a dedicated review document.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show that physical access is reviewed at least annually?

attributes.text: Data at rest is encrypted on all in-scope systems
attributes.typical_evidence: Database encryption settings (RDS encryption status, S3 default encryption, disk encryption config)
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: System configuration output shows encryption at rest enabled on all databases and storage systems containing sensitive data, using AES-256 or equivalent (AES-128 minimum). FAIL: Any database or storage system containing sensitive data has encryption at rest disabled, or uses a deprecated algorithm (DES, 3DES, RC4).

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A cloud console screenshot shows encryption enabled on the production database instance and on the storage bucket's default encryption setting, but the capture doesn't separately name the algorithm as AES-256 even though that is the service's documented default.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: when a managed service's encryption toggle is enabled and its documented default algorithm meets or exceeds the minimum, the capture doesn't need to spell out the algorithm name to pass.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The client wrote in a spreadsheet that all databases are encrypted at rest, with no console screenshot or export showing the actual encryption settings.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof for a configuration claim. The encryption-at-rest claim needs an actual console capture or export.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that data at rest is encrypted on all in-scope systems?

attributes.text: Data in transit is encrypted using TLS or equivalent for all in-scope connections
attributes.typical_evidence: TLS configuration (SSL Labs report, load balancer TLS settings, API endpoint HTTPS enforcement)
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: TLS configuration output (SSL Labs report, load balancer settings, or API endpoint config) shows TLS 1.2 or higher enforced. SSLv3, TLS 1.0, and TLS 1.1 are disabled. FAIL: Any in-scope endpoint supports TLS 1.1 or below, or SSLv3 is enabled.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A TLS scan of the production API endpoint shows only TLS 1.2 and 1.3 as supported protocols; the report doesn't include a separate line explicitly stating SSLv3 is disabled.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: a scan listing only modern TLS versions as supported IS proof that older protocols are disabled; absence of an explicit negative line item is not a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Engineering said in a standup that only modern TLS versions are allowed, with no scan report, load balancer configuration, or endpoint capture submitted.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. The TLS-version claim needs an actual scan output or configuration export.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that data in transit is encrypted using tls or equivalent for all in-scope connections?

attributes.text: Encryption algorithms and key lengths meet current standards
attributes.typical_evidence: Encryption configuration showing algorithm and key length (e.g., AES-256, RSA-2048+)
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Configuration output shows AES-256 (or AES-128 minimum) for data at rest, RSA-2048+ (or ECDSA P-256+) for key exchange, TLS 1.2+ for transit. Zero deprecated algorithms in use (DES, 3DES, MD5, SHA-1 for signatures, RC4). FAIL: Any deprecated algorithm is in use, or key lengths are below minimum (RSA <2048, AES <128).

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The transit-side TLS scan confirms compliant key exchange and cipher suites, but doesn't separately show a database encryption key length, which is covered by a different attribute's own evidence.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: don't import a neighboring attribute's evidence requirement into this one. If the algorithms and key lengths shown for this attribute's scope meet the standard, that is sufficient.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A security questionnaire response stated the company uses strong encryption and modern key lengths, with no actual configuration or scan output attached.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Written self-attestation without a capture is not configuration evidence. The algorithm and key-length claim needs an actual scan or configuration export.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that encryption algorithms?
Does the system configuration show that key lengths meet current standards?

attributes.text: Cryptographic keys are stored securely (not in source code or plaintext)
attributes.typical_evidence: KMS configuration, secrets manager setup, or code scan results showing no plaintext keys
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Configuration shows cryptographic keys stored in a KMS, secrets manager, or HSM. Code scan results or repository search confirms no plaintext keys in source code or config files. FAIL: Keys found in source code, config files, or stored in plaintext outside a secrets management system.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A code repository search for common secret patterns shows zero hits, and a separate secrets-manager dashboard screenshot shows the production signing key stored there; the two captures come from different tools rather than one unified report.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Judge the substance across the corpus, not whether it arrives in one unified report. A clean code-scan capture plus a secrets-manager capture together satisfy the attribute.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The engineering lead said on a call that keys are never hardcoded, with no code scan results or secrets manager configuration provided.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never evidence. The no-plaintext-keys claim needs an actual code scan output or secrets manager configuration capture.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that cryptographic keys are stored securely (not in source code or plaintext)?

attributes.text: Key rotation is performed or scheduled
attributes.typical_evidence: KMS key rotation settings or key rotation log showing rotation history
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: KMS configuration shows automatic key rotation enabled, OR manual rotation log shows rotation performed at least annually (rotation date within past 12 months). FAIL: No key rotation configured and no manual rotation evidence within the past 12 months.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A KMS console screenshot shows automatic key rotation toggled on for the production key; there is no separate rotation history log showing a completed rotation event yet.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Read the pass criteria precisely: automatic rotation enabled is an independent, sufficient pass path. Don't additionally demand a manual rotation history log when auto-rotation is on.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An admin said verbally that keys are rotated every year, with no KMS configuration screenshot or rotation log provided.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. The rotation claim needs an actual KMS config screenshot or a dated rotation log.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that key rotation is performed or scheduled?

attributes.text: Data disposal procedure exists
attributes.typical_evidence: Data disposal policy or procedure document covering physical and logical disposal
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Data disposal procedure document describes methods for data wiping (software-based) and hardware destruction (physical) for different asset types. FAIL: No data disposal procedure, or procedure does not describe specific wiping or destruction methods.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The company's asset handling policy has a short paragraph stating laptops are wiped via full-disk encryption key destruction before being recycled through a certified e-waste vendor; there are no other asset types since the company is fully cloud-based with no on-prem servers.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Solo/small-team proportionality: the procedure must be proportional to the entity's actual asset footprint. A short but concrete description covering the only asset type in use satisfies the attribute.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a data disposal policy or procedure document covering physical and logical disposal?

attributes.text: For each disposed asset: data is wiped or destroyed before disposal
attributes.typical_evidence: Certificate of destruction, data wipe log, or disposal vendor receipt
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if disposals occurred and the most recent disposal has a certificate of destruction, a data wipe log, or a disposal vendor receipt; if no disposals occurred, pass by default. FAIL if disposals occurred with no evidence of secure wiping or destruction.
