attributes.text: Privacy notice is published and accessible to data subjects before or at the time of data collection
attributes.typical_evidence: Published privacy notice URL, or documented delivery channel showing how data subjects receive the notice
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Privacy notice is published at a publicly accessible URL or provided to data subjects through a documented channel before or at the time of collection. FAIL: No privacy notice, or notice is not accessible to data subjects before collection.
attributes.na_condition: N/A if Privacy TSC not in scope

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A screenshot of the account sign-up flow shows a linked privacy notice presented to the user before they submit any personal information, but there is no separately hosted, publicly indexed privacy page.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Judge what the evidence shows: a documented delivery channel at the point of collection satisfies the criteria just as well as a standalone public URL. The sign-up flow screenshot demonstrates the notice was accessible before or at the time of collection, which is exactly what is required.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show that privacy notice is published?
Does the evidence show that accessible to data subjects before or at the time of data collection?

attributes.text: Notice covers all required elements: types of personal information collected, purposes of use, third-party disclosures, data subject rights, and entities/activities covered
attributes.typical_evidence: Privacy notice document reviewed for completeness of required elements
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Privacy notice contains all 5 required elements: (1) types of personal information collected, (2) purposes of use, (3) third-party disclosures, (4) data subject rights, (5) description of entities and activities covered. FAIL: Privacy notice is missing any of the 5 required elements.
attributes.na_condition: N/A if Privacy TSC not in scope

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The published privacy notice has a section titled 'Who We Share Data With' listing categories of vendors and partners receiving data, covering the third-party disclosure requirement without using that phrase verbatim.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: the criteria checks for the substantive presence of each required element, not a section titled with the exact regulatory phrase. A section describing who data is shared with satisfies the third-party disclosure requirement.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The published privacy notice covers the categories of personal information collected, why each is used, the named third parties it is shared with, and how learners exercise access and deletion rights. It never describes which entities or activities it covers; the company operates the tutoring marketplace and a separate assessment product under different brands.
calibration_examples.reasoning: All five elements are required and the description of covered entities and activities is the one most often absent, so a notice that reads as thorough can still fail on scope. Where an entity runs more than one product, a notice that never says which entities and activities it governs leaves a data subject unable to tell whether it applies to them.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show that notice covers all required elements: types of personal information collected, purposes of use, third-party disclosures, data subject rights?
Does the evidence show that entities/activities covered?

attributes.text: Notice is written in clear language and is current (dated within 24 months)
attributes.typical_evidence: Privacy notice showing date, plain-language structure, and headings
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Privacy notice uses plain language with headings, is dated or has a version date within the last 24 months, and is easily locatable (linked from footer, account settings, or sign-up flow). FAIL: Notice is undated, dated more than 24 months ago, or written entirely in legal jargon without plain-language summaries. FLAG: Notice uses technical terms without definitions, flag for CPA review.
attributes.na_condition: N/A if Privacy TSC not in scope

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The privacy notice was last substantively updated 10 months ago according to the internal version-history log in the CMS, but the public-facing page itself does not display a visible 'last updated' date to a casual reader.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verify the corpus before failing: the underlying version-history record establishes the notice is current within 24 months, which is what the criteria actually tests, even though that date is not surfaced as a footer timestamp on the page itself.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show that notice is written in clear language?
Does the evidence show that is current (dated within 24 months)?

attributes.text: Data subjects are informed when the notice changes, and prior versions are retained
attributes.typical_evidence: Version history or archive of prior privacy notices, and evidence of change notification (email, banner, or changelog)
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Prior versions of the privacy notice are retained (version history, archive, or web archive), AND a process exists for notifying data subjects of changes (email, banner, or documented procedure). FAIL: No prior versions retained, or no process for notifying data subjects of changes.
attributes.na_condition: N/A if Privacy TSC not in scope

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The privacy notice lives in the company's website content repository, where every prior version is preserved in commit history along with the date each change was published, and change announcements go out via an in-app banner; there is no formal public web-archive tool in use.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Solo/small-team proportionality: judge against a realistic minimum design rather than requiring a dedicated archiving product. A repository's version history preserving every prior notice, paired with a real in-app notification mechanism for changes, is a proportional and verifiable way to meet this requirement.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show that data subjects are informed when the notice changes?
Does the evidence show that prior versions are retained?

calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: the criteria requires that consequences of denying consent be communicated, not that they occupy a labeled section of their own. A brief but clear statement of what happens if consent is declined satisfies the substance of the requirement.

calibration_examples.reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: this is a config attribute, so the consent-capture mechanism and its stored records are the correct and sufficient evidence, not a placeholder awaiting a written policy. calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The client submitted a spreadsheet they manually typed logging 'consents received' by date and user name, with no export or screenshot from the actual consent-capture system or database.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that explicit consent is obtained separately for sensitive information?

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The evidence submitted for this attribute is a screenshot of a third-party analytics vendor's public page describing their own data-minimization practices, offered as proof of what personal information this org collects.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A provider's marketing or trust page is not this organization's own configuration. The criteria requires a comparison of this entity's actual collected data fields against its own privacy notice, not a vendor's unrelated public claims.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual consent records showing explicit consent for retention of personal information beyond the original collection purpose (not just a verbal description)?

attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Document describes a process for receiving, verifying identity, fulfilling, and responding to data subject access and correction requests, with defined response timeframe (default: 30 days). FAIL: No documented process for data subject access or correction requests.

calibration_examples.reasoning: A pass by default for a non-occurrence fails the moment the entity's own log shows the event occurred, whatever the client believes happened. Two requests were denied, and the messages sent carry neither a written reason nor any appeal instruction, which is precisely what this attribute requires a denial to include.

attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if the entity responds to access and correction requests within a defined timeframe (default: 30 days), and either no requests were received or the most recent request was responded to within the defined timeframe with personal information provided in an understandable format. FAIL if access and correction requests can be received with no defined response process or timeframe in place. TYPE II (over the period): If no requests were received, pass by default. calibration_examples.reasoning: At the design/Type I stage this attribute passes when a defined response timeframe is in place and no requests have been received, the criteria states this default explicitly. calibration_examples.reasoning: The requirement to communicate privacy requirements before disclosure applies to every third party that receives personal information, not to the ones large enough to have gone through procurement. calibration_examples.reasoning: A system export is system evidence regardless of its formatting or filename, it shows recipient, data type, date, and purpose exactly as required. Don't fail evidence for lacking a polished presentation when the substance is a genuine system-generated record.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A spreadsheet titled 'Vendor disclosures 2026' was typed up by the ops lead from memory, listing vendor names and rough dates, with no underlying system log or export to corroborate the entries.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet reconstructed from memory is not reliable disclosure proof, records need to be system-maintained or corroborated against an actual system view, with the recipient/data/date/purpose fields the criteria requires. calibration_examples.reasoning: Config attributes for a register pass on the mechanism existing, not on it having contents, the pass criteria explicitly treats an empty register as a pass when no breaches occurred. calibration_examples.evidence_summary: In an interview, the head of engineering said 'we'd log any breach in our internal tracker if one happened,' but no screenshot, export, or actual tracker view was provided.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never config evidence, a described capability with no system capture to back it up doesn't demonstrate the mechanism actually exists. The attribute needs a record or screenshot of the tracker itself, not an assurance about it.

attributes.typical_evidence: Third-party privacy assessment records and contractual breach notification clauses for each recipient of personal information
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if the entity assesses privacy compliance of third parties receiving personal information and obtains breach reporting commitments, and either no third-party disclosures occurred or the most recent third party has a privacy compliance assessment on file and a contractual commitment to report unauthorized disclosures. calibration_examples.reasoning: Compensating controls are a legitimate pass path at design stage, for a solo founder, a documented review of a vendor's public security attestation plus the DPA's breach clause stands in for a formal assessment questionnaire. calibration_examples.reasoning: Identification of breach-reporting requirements passes on substance regardless of the document's title or location. The runbook table actually names the regulatory timelines, recipients, and contractual obligations the criteria asks for, so failing it for not being a standalone titled document imports a form requirement the attribute doesn't state.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show that applicable breach reporting requirements are identified (regulatory?

attributes.text: Breach notification procedures define timelines, responsible parties, and notification content
attributes.typical_evidence: Breach notification procedure with defined timelines, responsible parties, and notification templates or content requirements
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Procedure defines notification timelines meeting regulatory requirements, identifies responsible parties for executing notifications, and describes required notification content. calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The breach notification timeline, responsible-party assignment, and required notification content are all defined within a section of the company's broader incident response plan rather than in a standalone breach-notification document.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Never import a requirement the attribute text doesn't state, nothing in the criteria requires a standalone document, only that timelines, responsible parties, and content are defined somewhere. No timeline, no named role, and no description of what a notification must contain appears anywhere in the plan or its appendices.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A commitment to comply is not a procedure, and this attribute requires timelines, responsible parties, and notification content, none of which a sentence restating the legal obligation supplies. calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism, the attribute asks for personal information types, handling processes, and third parties involved to be documented, and a maintained Notion data map does exactly that. The specific artifact name (ROPA) is typical evidence, not a required label.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The company has never received a request for an accounting of personal information held and disclosed.

attributes.typical_evidence: Data quality controls documentation showing validation at collection, self-service update capability, or periodic data quality checks
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Document describes processes for maintaining personal information accuracy and completeness, at minimum data validation at collection points and a mechanism for data subjects to update their information (self-service or request-based). attributes.na_condition: N/A if Privacy TSC not in scope

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The signup form enforces required-field and email-format validation at collection, and the account settings page lets users edit their own profile data afterward; both are described briefly in the engineering wiki rather than a standalone 'Data Quality Policy.'
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism, the pass criteria asks for validation at collection plus a self-service update mechanism, both of which are present and documented, just not under a dedicated policy title. calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The data handling document describes validation at collection in detail: email verification, phone format checks, and duplicate detection on employer records. calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A cropped GitHub branch protection screenshot shows the 'Include administrators' toggle in the on position, but the rest of the settings page is cut off from the capture.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A live capture plainly showing the substance passes even if it is not a full-page screenshot. The visible toggle is the exact setting the attribute tests, so a partial crop that still shows it is sufficient.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The founder verbally confirms in the review call that 'admin enforcement is always on for the production branch,' with no GitHub settings export submitted.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never config evidence. The administrator-enforcement setting must be shown in an actual branch protection configuration export, not asserted in conversation.

coverage_checks.question: Does the branch protection configuration show that enforcement applies to administrators with no bypass?

attributes.text: Required status checks must pass before a change can merge to a production branch
attributes.typical_evidence: Branch protection required status checks configuration listing the checks that must pass, plus the CI workflow definition that produces them
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Branch protection configuration lists one or more required status checks that must report success before a merge is allowed, and the corresponding CI workflow exists and runs on changes to the production branch. FAIL: No status checks are required for merging, or required checks are configured but the referenced CI workflow does not exist or does not run.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Branch protection configuration for the production branch requires only a single 'build' status check to pass before merge, and the corresponding CI workflow runs on every pull request.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: the pass criteria requires 'one or more' required status checks, not a specific number or a comprehensive test suite. A single enforced, functioning check satisfies the attribute as written.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A CI workflow file defining a test suite exists in the repository, but the branch protection settings export shows required_status_checks is null, meaning nothing is actually enforced at merge time.
calibration_examples.reasoning: The mere existence of a CI workflow is not the same as the workflow being required for merge. The system configuration must actually show the check listed as required, and here it does not.

coverage_checks.question: Does the configuration show that one or more status checks are required to pass before merging to production?
Does the evidence show the CI workflow that produces the required checks exists and runs on changes?

attributes.text: For each merged change: the change is traceable and carries a description and passing required checks
attributes.typical_evidence: Merged pull request or merge request records showing a description, the passing required status checks, and the commit history linking the change to the production branch
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if each inspected merged change has a description explaining the change, shows the required status checks passed before the merge, and is traceable to its commit history on the production branch. FAIL if any inspected change has no description, merged with failing or missing required checks, or cannot be traced to a merge. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every merged change across the period carries a description and passing required checks; isolated misses in an otherwise working practice are an exception, not a gap; systematic absence of descriptions or of passing checks is a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: For a solo-developer company, the merged pull requests show a description of the change and passing required CI checks, but were self-approved by the same developer who authored them, since no second engineer exists.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Never import a neighbor attribute's requirement: this attribute only requires a description, passing required checks, and traceability, not a second-person approval, which belongs to a separate peer-review control. Judged against its own text, the merges pass.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Each of the three inspected merged changes has a clear description and a green status check visible on the pull request. On one of them the merge commit is timestamped 14:02 and the required test run finished at 14:41, having been triggered on the main branch after the merge.
calibration_examples.reasoning: The checks have to pass before the merge, because a check that runs afterwards tells the entity what it shipped rather than gating whether it ships. A green badge read at fieldwork time hides the ordering, so the timestamps are the evidence, not the badge.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual merged change record such as a pull request or merge request (not just a verbal description)?
Does the record show the merged change carries a description of what changed?
Does the record show the required status checks passed before the merge?

attributes.text: A post deployment verification practice confirms each deployed change works as intended
attributes.typical_evidence: Records of checks performed after deployment such as monitoring dashboards, health check results, smoke test output, or deployment logs showing verification after release
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if {company_name} performs a defined verification after each deployment such as automated health checks, smoke tests, or a monitoring review, and evidence shows this was done for a recent deployment. FAIL if there is no verification after deployment, or it is only described verbally with no supporting record. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every deployment across the period shows verification was performed; isolated misses in an otherwise working practice are an exception, not a gap; systematic absence of verification after deployment is a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The deployment platform's dashboard automatically runs a post-deploy health check and shows a green 'Deployment Ready' status with response-time metrics for the most recent release, captured as a screenshot.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A live capture plainly showing the substance passes even without a separately written 'verification log.' An automated platform health check tied to the deployment is exactly the kind of record the attribute asks for.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The deployment pipeline definition includes a smoke test stage with real assertions against the ticketing checkout path. The run log for the most recent production deployment shows that stage as 'skipped', because it is configured to run only when a manual flag is set, and no monitoring review or other verification was recorded for that deployment.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A verification practice has to have been performed for a recent deployment, so a configured stage that did not run is a defined intention rather than evidence. A conditional gate that defaults to skipped will be skipped exactly when it matters, which is why the attribute asks for the run and not the configuration.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a record of verification performed after a deployment such as health check results, smoke test output, or a monitoring review?
Does the record show the verification confirmed the deployed change was working as intended?

attributes.text: A current inventory of every device that accesses production is maintained
attributes.typical_evidence: Device inventory listing each production-accessing laptop and the person assigned to it, dated recently
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: An inventory lists every device used to access production, each tied to a named owner, and the device count is at least the number of people who access production. FAIL: No inventory exists, or a device known to access production is missing from it, or the inventory is undated and cannot be confirmed as current. NOTE: For a founder-managed environment the inventory may be a simple maintained list; what matters is that it is complete and current, not its format.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A two-founder company maintains a simple shared spreadsheet listing each founder's laptop, serial number, and owner, updated within the past week.
calibration_examples.reasoning: For a founder-managed environment the attribute's own note allows the inventory to be a simple maintained list. A current, complete spreadsheet tying each device to its owner passes on that proportional basis rather than being gapped for lacking a formal asset-management tool.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The device inventory lists nine laptops, each tied to a named owner and updated last month. The identity provider shows twelve accounts with production access; three of those people appear nowhere in the device inventory, and two of them are contractors known to work from their own machines.
calibration_examples.reasoning: This attribute sets an explicit floor, that the device count is at least the number of people who access production, so a well maintained list that is short of that floor still fails. Devices missing from the inventory are usually personal or contractor machines, which are the ones no endpoint control reaches.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a maintained list of devices that access production?
Does the inventory tie each device to a named owner and cover everyone who accesses production?

attributes.text: Disk encryption is enabled on every device that accesses production
attributes.typical_evidence: Per device command output or screenshot showing FileVault or BitLocker on, one per device in the inventory
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: For every device in the production-accessing inventory, actual command output or a screenshot of that output shows full disk encryption enabled (FileVault on, or BitLocker protection on and 100 percent encrypted). Evidence count matches the inventory. FAIL: Any inventoried device lacks encryption evidence, or any device shows encryption off or partial. NOTE: A founder-authored spreadsheet asserting encryption is not acceptable; the proof is the device's own command output or a screenshot of it.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Disk-encryption command output was captured for both founders' current laptops in the inventory, but a third, older laptop that was retired and removed from the device inventory before the test date has no capture.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Encryption evidence is measured against the current inventory, not a device already removed from service. A retired laptop no longer in the production-accessing inventory is outside the population, so full coverage of the two active inventoried devices passes.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A founder submits a short written statement asserting 'both our laptops have FileVault turned on' instead of an actual command output or screenshot from each device.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A founder-authored assertion is explicitly not acceptable proof for this attribute; the required evidence is the device's own command output or a screenshot of it. A typed claim with no real system capture gaps.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include actual disk encryption command output or a screenshot of it for each device in the inventory?
Does every device's output show full disk encryption enabled?

attributes.text: Screen lock is enabled on every device that accesses production
attributes.typical_evidence: Per device command output or screenshot showing password required after a short idle timeout, one per device in the inventory
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: For every device in the production-accessing inventory, command output or a screenshot shows screen lock enabled with a password required and an idle timeout of 15 minutes or less. Evidence count matches the inventory. FAIL: Any inventoried device lacks screen lock evidence, or shows screen lock disabled, or shows an idle timeout longer than 15 minutes. NOTE: The proof is the device's own setting output, not a verbal or written claim.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Screenshots of each inventoried device's system settings show screen lock enabled with the timeout set to 'immediately,' rather than a specific minute count listed in a field.
calibration_examples.reasoning: An 'immediately' lock setting is strictly tighter than the 15-minute maximum the attribute allows, so the live capture plainly satisfies the requirement. No numeric minute value needs to appear separately when the setting is visibly within bound.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A founder describes in a Slack message that screen lock is enabled on all company devices, but no screenshots or command output from the devices themselves were captured.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A written or verbal assertion is never a substitute for the device's own setting output, which this attribute requires. Without an actual screenshot or command result per inventoried device, it gaps pending real evidence.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include actual screen lock setting output or a screenshot of it for each device in the inventory?
Does every device's output show a password required with an idle timeout of 15 minutes or less?

attributes.text: Automatic operating system and software updates are enabled on every device that accesses production
attributes.typical_evidence: Per device command output or screenshot showing automatic update settings enabled, one per device in the inventory
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: For every device in the production-accessing inventory, command output or a screenshot shows automatic operating system and software updates enabled. Evidence count matches the inventory. FAIL: Any inventoried device lacks update setting evidence, or shows automatic updates disabled or deferred indefinitely. NOTE: The proof is the device's own update configuration output, not a written assertion.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Update-setting screenshots show 'Automatically keep my Mac up to date' turned on for each inventoried device, but one screenshot was captured a week before the as-of test date rather than on that exact date.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A persistent toggle setting captured shortly before the test date, with no evidence of any subsequent change, still reflects the as-of-date configuration. A minor capture-date gap does not undermine evidence of a standing setting, so it passes.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A founder provides a typed list stating 'all devices set to auto-update: yes' with no accompanying screenshots or command output from the devices.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A typed assertion is explicitly not acceptable here; the attribute requires the device's own update-configuration output. A written list with no real capture gaps pending device-level evidence.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include actual automatic update setting output or a screenshot of it for each device in the inventory?
Does every device's output show automatic operating system and software updates enabled?

attributes.text: A documented practice requires periodic access self-review anchored on system-generated exports
attributes.typical_evidence: Written access management practice stating the review cadence and that reviews start from user lists exported from each system
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: A written practice requires access to be reviewed on a defined periodic cadence and states that each review is based on a user list pulled from the system itself rather than a list written from memory. FAIL: No documented practice, or the practice does not state a cadence, or it relies on self-attestation without system exports.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A draft onboarding runbook includes a line 'Access review cadence: TBD, review anchored on exports' with the rest of the document still marked as a work-in-progress outline with no owner or adoption date.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A draft with an unresolved placeholder is not an adopted practice. A 'TBD' cadence means the practice does not actually state a cadence as the attribute requires, regardless of language elsewhere in the draft that sounds compliant.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a written practice for periodic access review?
Does the practice state that reviews are anchored on user lists pulled from each system?

attributes.text: For each review period: a self-review was performed at least quarterly with a dated record
attributes.typical_evidence: Dated review records showing reviews occurred at least once per quarter across the timeframe
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if a dated record shows a self-review was performed within the last 12 months at the entity's stated cadence, at least quarterly. FAIL if no dated review record exists or the most recent review predates the stated cadence. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every review period shows a dated review at least quarterly across the period; isolated misses in an otherwise working practice are an exception, not a gap; systematic absence, such as only one review across a full year, is a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A two-person company logs its self-reviews as dated entries in a shared Notion page roughly every three months, with no formal audit-tooling export, but the dates show consistent quarterly spacing over the year.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Judge against proportional practice for a small team: a consistently dated informal log meeting the stated quarterly cadence is a legitimate pass path, not a requirement for dedicated compliance tooling. The pass rests on the dated records showing reviews at the required cadence, proportional to team size.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The access management policy states the founder self-reviews access quarterly. One dated review record was provided, a spreadsheet of all accounts reviewed seven months ago, with no review recorded since.
calibration_examples.reasoning: The cadence the entity set for itself is the benchmark this attribute measures against, not the twelve month outer bound. A single review seven months old means at least one quarterly cycle passed with no review at all, so the practice as stated is not being followed.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include dated records of reviews actually performed?
Do the review dates show a review at least once per quarter across the timeframe?

attributes.text: For each review: each review is anchored on a system-generated access export for every in-scope system
attributes.typical_evidence: Review records with the attached or referenced system pulled user lists for each in-scope system
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if the most recent review attaches or references a user list exported from each in-scope system, and the exports are system-generated rather than typed from memory. FAIL if any in-scope system is missing its export, or the access list is a self-authored spreadsheet with no system origin. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every review in the period attaches a system-generated export for every in-scope system; isolated misses in an otherwise working practice are an exception, not a gap; systematic absence, such as reviews resting on hand-typed lists, is a gap. NOTE: A founder-authored spreadsheet is not a system-generated export; acceptable proof is output pulled from the system such as an API result, an admin console export, or a screenshot of the system's own user list.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The quarterly self-review is based on a spreadsheet the founder typed from memory listing current employees and their access, which happens to match the actual production user list.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A founder-authored spreadsheet is not a system-generated export, even when its contents happen to be accurate. The attribute requires the review to be anchored on output pulled from the system itself, such as an API result or admin console export, not a hand-typed list.

coverage_checks.question: Does each review include a user list pulled from the system for each in-scope system?
Are the access lists system-generated exports rather than lists typed by the founder?

attributes.text: For each review: unexpected access found is noted and remediated with a dated record
attributes.typical_evidence: Review records showing any unexpected accounts or permissions identified and the dated removal or adjustment
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if the most recent review shows either that no unexpected access was found, or that each unexpected account or permission was removed or adjusted with a dated record. FAIL if unexpected access is noted with no evidence of remediation. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if across all reviews in the period every noted item of unexpected access was remediated with a dated record; isolated delays in an otherwise working practice are an exception, not a gap; unremediated access left standing is a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An unexpected admin grant found during the quarterly review was revoked directly in the identity provider the same day, evidenced by a timestamped screenshot of the access removal, with no separate remediation ticket filed.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: a timestamped system screenshot showing the access was actually removed is a dated record of remediation and does not require a separate ticket to be credible. The substance, dated removal of the unexpected access, is what the attribute tests.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The most recent access review spreadsheet has a 'flagged' column with three entries marked 'remove, no longer needs access', including a former contractor's account. The identity provider export taken the week of fieldwork still shows all three accounts active with the same permissions, and no removal ticket or change record was provided.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Noticing unexpected access is the first half of this attribute and remediating it with a dated record is the other half, so a review that identifies accounts and changes nothing fails. A flag that outlives the review is evidence the review is a formality rather than a control.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual dated review record?
Does the record show whether any unexpected access was found?
For any unexpected access found, does the evidence show it was removed or adjusted with a date?

attributes.text: Administrative and deployment access to the production hosting platform is restricted to authorized personnel through defined member roles
attributes.typical_evidence: Export or screenshot of the hosting platform organization members list showing each member and their assigned role
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: The platform members list shows every member mapped to a defined role, production deploy or admin privileges are limited to authorized personnel, and no unknown or former personnel retain access. FAIL: Members hold production admin or deploy access without authorization, former personnel remain listed, or all members share a single unrestricted admin role. NOTE: Whether those members also authenticate with multi factor authentication is evaluated separately under the entity's access management controls; this attribute tests role restriction on the hosting platform itself.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The platform members export shows every member mapped to a role, and a former contractor's account is already removed from the org, but the capture was taken from the billing page rather than a dedicated members page.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Judge what the evidence shows, not the exact page it came from. If the capture clearly lists members and roles with no former personnel retained, the source page it was captured from is immaterial.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The admin said on a call that old members were cleaned up last month, with no members-list export or screenshot provided.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. The role-restriction claim needs an actual export or screenshot of the current members list.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include the hosting platform members list showing each member and their assigned role?

attributes.text: Production deployments are gated so that only approved sources promote to production, and preview or branch deployments are isolated from production
attributes.typical_evidence: Deployment protection or git integration settings showing the production branch or protected environment and its promotion controls, plus the preview deployment configuration
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Platform settings show production is deployed only from an approved branch or protected environment, promotion to production requires an approval or a protected trigger, and preview or branch deployments run in isolation from production data and credentials. FAIL: Any commit or contributor can deploy directly to production without gating, or preview deployments share production data or credentials.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The git integration settings show production deploys only from the main branch with required review before merge, and preview deployments run per-branch with separate environment variables; the screenshot doesn't separately label a protected-environment toggle, though the branch and review gating is visible.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: a capture plainly showing branch-restricted deploys gated by required review, with preview environments isolated, passes even if a specific named feature isn't separately itemized.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The client wrote in a spreadsheet that only the main branch can deploy to production, with no screenshot or export of the actual deployment protection settings.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof of a configuration claim. The deployment gating needs an actual settings capture from the hosting platform.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show that production deployments are gated to approved sources and that preview deployments are isolated from production?

attributes.text: Production secrets and environment variables are stored in the platform managed secret store and scoped to the production environment
attributes.typical_evidence: Environment variable listing per environment, for example the output of the platform command that lists production variables with values hidden, showing production secrets are defined in the platform and separated by environment
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: The environment variable configuration shows production secrets are held in the platform managed store, scoped to the production environment, and not shared into preview or development environments, with secret values masked in the listing. FAIL: Production secrets are absent from the platform store, implying they live in code or in shared files, or the same secrets are exposed to non production environments. NOTE: The listing must be a per environment configuration output, not a client authored spreadsheet of variable names.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The platform's own CLI environment-variable listing for production shows secret values masked and distinct from the preview and development listings, with no overlapping variable names, captured via the platform's export command.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: separate, masked per-environment listings with no overlapping secrets between production and preview or development IS the evidence of scoping; nothing further needs to be spelled out.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The client typed a spreadsheet of environment variable names claiming they live in the platform's secret store, with no captured export or screenshot of the actual configuration.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet of variable names is explicitly not acceptable for this attribute; only a real per-environment configuration export or screenshot corroborates the secrets-scoping claim.

coverage_checks.question: Does the configuration show production secrets stored in the platform secret store and scoped to the production environment?

attributes.text: Production endpoints are served over enforced HTTPS with valid TLS certificates
attributes.typical_evidence: Certificate listing for the production custom domains, or response headers from the production endpoint showing HTTPS and certificate validity
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: The certificate listing shows valid unexpired TLS certificates for every production custom domain, and requests to the production endpoint are served over HTTPS while plain HTTP is redirected or refused. FAIL: A production domain has no valid certificate, a certificate is expired, or the endpoint serves content over unencrypted HTTP.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A live browser network capture shows a valid certificate padlock and a 301 redirect from HTTP to HTTPS on the production domain, but the file isn't formatted as a formal certificate listing export.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Judge the substance a live capture shows, not its format; a capture demonstrating a valid certificate and enforced HTTPS redirect passes regardless of whether it looks like a formal certificate listing.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The client wrote in a security questionnaire response that SSL is enabled, with no certificate listing, scan output, or screenshot attached.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Written self-attestation without a capture is not configuration evidence. The TLS claim needs an actual certificate listing or endpoint scan showing validity and enforcement.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show valid TLS certificates for the production domains and HTTPS enforced on the production endpoint?

attributes.text: Provider audit logs are enabled across the production platforms and services in scope
attributes.typical_evidence: Logging configuration or settings for each in scope provider, covering the hosting platform audit log, the managed database logs, and the authentication provider logs, showing logging is turned on
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: The logging configuration for every in scope provider, including the hosting platform, the managed database, and the authentication provider, shows audit or activity logging enabled and capturing authentication, access change, and administrative events. FAIL: Any in scope provider has audit logging disabled or not configured. NOTE: Because these are managed services, a settings screenshot or provider export is acceptable system state evidence; a client authored list of what is logged is not.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A screenshot of the Supabase project's logs dashboard and Vercel's deployment log settings shows both providers actively capturing authentication and admin activity, but neither uses the exact term 'audit log' in its UI.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: a managed provider's activity or event logging that substantively captures the required categories satisfies the attribute even when the provider's own UI does not use the words 'audit log.'

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A client-authored table lists each provider (hosting, database, auth) with a checkmark for 'logging enabled,' but no settings screenshot or export from any of the providers themselves was submitted.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Because these are managed services, a client-authored list of what is logged is explicitly not acceptable; each provider's own settings screen or export must be captured to verify logging is actually turned on.

coverage_checks.question: Does the configuration show audit or activity logging enabled on each in scope provider?

attributes.text: Audit log retention on each in scope provider meets the retention period defined in the entity's logging policy
attributes.typical_evidence: Log retention setting for each provider, for example the retention configuration shown in the platform or database dashboard, alongside the entity's documented retention period
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: The retention setting shown for each in scope provider meets or exceeds the retention period defined in the entity's logging or data retention policy. FAIL: A provider retains audit logs for less than the entity's defined period, or retention is left at a default shorter than the policy requires. NOTE: Compare the configured retention against the entity's own documented period; do not assume a period the entity has not defined.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The hosting provider's dashboard shows log retention set to 'unlimited,' a non-numeric default option, against an entity policy requiring one year of retention.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: an unlimited or maximum-available retention setting necessarily exceeds any finite defined period and should be read as satisfying the requirement rather than failed for not stating a specific day count.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The provider's dashboard shows a default 90-day log retention setting, and the entity's own logging policy defines a 180-day minimum, but the AI compared the provider's setting only against the generic 90-day floor and not against the entity's own longer policy.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Compare the configured retention against the entity's own documented period, not an assumed generic floor; a setting that meets a general minimum but falls short of the entity's own stricter policy is a gap.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show each provider's log retention setting meeting the entity's defined retention period?

attributes.text: Audit logs are protected from tampering and premature deletion
attributes.typical_evidence: Provider configuration showing logs are read only to normal users, deletion or purge restricted to administrators, or immutability and retention lock settings
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: The provider configuration shows audit logs cannot be edited by normal users and that deletion or purge is restricted to administrators or governed by a retention lock. FAIL: Any user can delete or alter audit logs, or logs can be purged before the retention period ends without restriction.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A screenshot of the database provider's role permissions shows that only the service role can query historical logs and no delete or purge API is exposed to organization members, but there is no separate 'retention lock' toggle.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A compensating combination of restricted read access and no exposed deletion path is a legitimate pass path when verifiable, even without the single named immutability feature the typical evidence describes.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An internal IT note states 'no one can delete our audit logs,' but no screenshot of the provider's actual role or permission configuration was submitted.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal or written assertions are never config evidence; the provider's own permission settings must be captured to confirm logs cannot be altered or deleted.

coverage_checks.question: Does the configuration show audit logs protected from edit and from unrestricted deletion?

attributes.text: Provider audit logs are reviewed on a defined cadence or connected to alerting so that anomalies are surfaced
attributes.typical_evidence: Records of periodic log review, such as dated review notes, tickets, or sign offs, or configuration routing provider logs into an alerting or monitoring destination
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if there is either a defined log review cadence with at least one dated review record, or configuration showing provider audit logs are routed into an alerting or monitoring destination that notifies personnel. FAIL if enabled logs are never reviewed and are not connected to any alerting. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every review period shows the review was performed on the defined cadence, or the alerting connection was in place throughout the period; isolated misses in an otherwise working practice are an exception, not a gap; systematic absence is a gap. NOTE: The triage and severity handling of individual alerts is evaluated separately under the entity's security alerting control; this attribute tests only that the platform native logs are actually consumed rather than left write only.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: No dated manual log review record exists, but a configuration screenshot shows the provider's audit logs are piped into a monitoring platform that pages on-call staff for anomalies.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Compensating controls are a legitimate pass path at design stage: a live alerting connection that surfaces anomalies satisfies the attribute just as well as a manual dated review record, since the goal is that logs are actually consumed rather than left write-only.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The provider console shows audit logging enabled across all regions and delivering to a retention bucket. There is no defined review cadence and no dated review record. The monitoring tool's alert rules were exported and cover application error rates and endpoint latency only, with no rule reading the provider audit log.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Collecting a log is not reviewing it, and this attribute is satisfied by a review cadence with a dated record or by alerting that actually reads the log. Retention with nothing watching means an anomaly is discoverable afterwards rather than surfaced, which is the difference the attribute is drawing.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include dated records of periodic log review or configuration routing provider logs into alerting?

attributes.text: Provider managed data stores have point in time recovery or automated backups enabled, with a defined retention period and geographically separate storage
attributes.typical_evidence: Backup or point in time recovery configuration for each provider managed data store showing the feature is enabled, the retention period, and the storage region
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: The configuration for every provider managed data store shows point in time recovery or automated backups enabled, a retention period that meets the entity's defined requirement, and backup or replica storage in a region separate from the primary. FAIL: Any provider managed data store has backups or point in time recovery disabled, retention below the entity's defined requirement, or backups stored only in the same region as the primary. NOTE: This must be the provider's own configuration output or dashboard setting, not a client authored description of the backup arrangement.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A managed Postgres provider's dashboard screenshot shows point-in-time recovery enabled with a 14-day retention window and a read replica listed in a different region, but the capture was submitted as a plain 'database settings' screenshot with no callout of the region field.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A live capture plainly showing the substance passes even if each element is not separately itemized. The dashboard already shows PITR enabled, retention, and a separate-region replica, which is exactly what the attribute requires.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The internal runbook states 'our database provider automatically handles backups and recovery for us,' with no actual provider dashboard screenshot or configuration export submitted.
calibration_examples.reasoning: The attribute's own pass criteria explicitly requires the provider's own configuration output, not a client-authored description of the arrangement. A written assurance about the provider's behavior is not the same as showing the provider's actual settings.

coverage_checks.question: Does the configuration show point in time recovery or automated backups enabled with retention and separate region for each managed data store?

attributes.text: For each restoration test: recovery from a provider managed backup was tested successfully within the last 12 months, with date and scope documented

attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if a restoration test record dated within the past 12 months shows a successful recovery from a provider managed backup, with the scope, date, and outcome documented. FAIL if there is no restoration test within the past 12 months, or the record shows the restoration failed. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every restoration test in the period completed successfully with documented scope and outcome; isolated misses in an otherwise working practice are an exception, not a gap; systematic absence is a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An engineer states in the review call that 'we tested restoring from a backup a few months ago and it worked fine,' but no dated restoration record, dashboard export, or ticket documenting the test was submitted.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never a substitute for a documented record. The attribute requires an actual restoration test record showing the date, the data store restored, and the outcome, not a recollection offered in conversation.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual restoration test record with date and scope, not just a verbal description?
Does the record show a successful recovery from a provider managed backup within the last 12 months?

attributes.text: Recovery steps for restoring the provider managed data stores are documented
attributes.typical_evidence: A written recovery procedure or runbook describing how to restore each provider managed data store from its backup or point in time recovery
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: A written procedure describes, for each provider managed data store, how to restore from backup or point in time recovery, including who performs it and the target recovery point. FAIL: No documented restoration procedure exists, or the procedure omits the in scope data stores. NOTE: This is the specific restoration runbook for the managed data stores; the entity's overall continuity and disaster recovery plan is evaluated separately.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The restoration steps for the managed database exist as inline comments in the infrastructure repository's README rather than as a separately titled 'runbook' document, but they clearly walk through how to restore from the provider's point-in-time recovery.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: documented recovery steps satisfy the attribute regardless of where they physically live, as long as they clearly describe how to restore the in-scope data store from backup. A README section carries the same weight as a standalone runbook file.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The recovery runbook covers the managed Postgres instance thoroughly: point in time restore steps, who performs them, and a one hour recovery point target. The object storage bucket holding every published audio file and the managed Redis instance holding session and queue state appear nowhere in the runbook, though both are listed as provider managed stores in the architecture document.
calibration_examples.reasoning: The procedure has to reach each provider managed data store the entity depends on, so depth on the database does not cover the stores left out. Object storage is usually the one omitted and usually the one holding the content the service exists to deliver.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a written procedure for restoring each managed data store from backup?

FAIL: No inventory of hosted AI model providers exists, or the inventory omits the data each provider receives.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The AI provider inventory is a live Notion database with columns for provider, data categories, and sending system; the evidence pulled was a screenshot of that database rather than an exported document.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Live system screenshots are valid system evidence regardless of format. The database plainly names each provider, the data it receives, and the sending system, which is what the attribute requires.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an inventory listing each hosted AI model provider along with the data it receives and the system that sends it?

attributes.na_condition: No hosted AI model provider processes customer data; all providers process only the entity's internal data

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Engineering states verbally that OpenAI's standard business-tier terms apply to the account sending customer data, but no signed agreement or DPA was pulled from the account or contract records.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never adequate evidence of a governing agreement. The attribute requires the actual signed agreement or DPA on file for the provider, not an assertion that standard terms apply.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a signed agreement or data processing addendum for each provider that processes customer data?

attributes.text: Model training and data use terms are identified for each hosted AI model provider

attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: For each provider the entity has identified and documented whether submitted inputs and outputs are used to train the provider's models and the applicable retention terms, referencing the governing agreement or the published terms in effect. FAIL: Model training or data use terms are not identified for one or more providers, or the terms rest only on an unreferenced assertion.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The documented training-terms summary for Anthropic cites the default API policy that inputs and outputs are not used for training, linking to the current published terms, but there is no separately negotiated contract addendum.
calibration_examples.reasoning: The pass criteria explicitly accept identification referencing the governing agreement or the published terms in effect, not only a negotiated addendum. A dated citation to the applicable default terms satisfies the attribute.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The AI provider inventory's training column reads 'No, does not train on our data' for all three providers, each citing the provider's public marketing page. No agreement, order form, or terms reference is recorded, and one of the three is used on a free tier whose published terms differ from the enterprise terms quoted on that page.
calibration_examples.reasoning: The terms that bind are the ones in the governing agreement for the tier actually in use, which is why this attribute asks the determination to reference it. A marketing page describes the vendor's usual posture and can be accurate in general while being wrong for the plan the entity is on, and retention terms are missing from the record entirely.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show, for each provider, whether submitted data is used to train the provider's models and the applicable retention terms, with a reference to the governing terms?

attributes.text: Hosted AI model providers that receive customer data are disclosed in the entity's subprocessor list
attributes.typical_evidence: Published or customer-facing subprocessor list showing the AI model providers that receive customer data and the purpose of processing

FAIL: A provider that receives customer data is absent from the subprocessor list.
