attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if the most recent user access review record shows contractor accounts with production or customer data access were included in the reviewed population and evaluated, or no such contractors existed as of the review. FAIL if contractor accounts existed but were excluded from the review population. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if contractor accounts were included in every user access review performed during the period; an isolated omission of a single account in an otherwise complete review is an exception, not a gap; systematic exclusion of contractors is a gap.
attributes.na_condition: Entity engages no contractors with production or customer data access

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The quarterly access review spreadsheet has separate tabs for 'Employees' and 'Contractors/Vendors,' and the contractor tab was reviewed and signed off in the same cycle as the employee tab.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline means checking whether contractor accounts were evaluated, not whether they sit in the same tab as employees. A separately organized but equally reviewed contractor population satisfies the requirement that contractors be included in the reviewed population.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual user access review record, not just a claim that reviews happen?
Does the review record show contractor accounts were included in the reviewed population and evaluated alongside employees?

attributes.text: The health and uptime of production systems are continuously monitored
attributes.typical_evidence: Monitoring platform showing active uptime or health checks against production services
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Monitoring configuration shows active uptime or health checks running against the main production services, such as synthetic checks, endpoint pings, or health probes. FAIL: No uptime or health monitoring configured for production services. NOTE: Internal metric dashboards without any uptime or health check do not satisfy this on their own.
attributes.na_condition: N/A if Availability TSC not in scope

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A solo-founder company uses a free-tier uptime checker pinging its health endpoint every five minutes, rather than an enterprise synthetic-monitoring suite.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Solo-founder proportionality: judge against the minimum acceptable design for a 1-2 person company. A lightweight external health check hitting production satisfies continuous uptime monitoring at that scale.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An internal Datadog dashboard shows CPU, memory, and request-rate metrics for production, and this was credited as uptime monitoring even though no synthetic check or health endpoint probe exists.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Internal metric dashboards without any uptime or health check do not satisfy this attribute on their own, per its explicit note. Resource metrics are not the same as an external check confirming the service is actually reachable.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include configuration showing uptime or health checks running against production systems?

attributes.text: Alerts notify responsible personnel when availability degrades or an outage is detected
attributes.typical_evidence: Alert rule configuration showing availability triggers and notification targets
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Alert configuration shows rules that trigger on availability signals such as a failed health check, endpoint downtime, or elevated error rate, with a defined notification target such as paging, chat, or on call routing. FAIL: No availability alerts configured, or alerts exist but route to no active recipient. NOTE: An alert that only records an event without notifying anyone does not satisfy this.
attributes.na_condition: N/A if Availability TSC not in scope

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Availability alerts route to a shared team Slack channel watched by a rotating on-call engineer, rather than a named individual via a paging tool.
calibration_examples.reasoning: The pass criteria accept chat or on-call routing as a valid notification target, not only individual paging. A monitored shared channel is a defined recipient satisfying the attribute.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An availability alert monitor shows a 'triggered' event history for a past outage, but its notification channel field is blank, meaning the event was logged with no one actually notified.
calibration_examples.reasoning: An alert that only records an event without notifying anyone does not satisfy this attribute, per its explicit note. Evidence of a triggered state is not evidence anyone was alerted.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include alert configuration that notifies personnel when availability degrades or an outage occurs?

attributes.text: Availability incidents such as outages or degradations are responded to and resolved
attributes.typical_evidence: Incident records for availability events showing detection, response actions, and resolution timestamps
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if the entity has a defined path for responding to availability incidents, and if any outages have occurred each has an incident record showing response and resolution; if no availability incidents have occurred, pass by default on the defined path. FAIL if there is no defined response path, or an outage occurred with no response record. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every availability incident in the period shows timely response and resolution with detection and resolution timestamps recorded; isolated misses in an otherwise working practice are an exception, not a gap; systematic absence is a gap. FAIL if incidents routinely lack response or resolution records.
attributes.na_condition: N/A if Availability TSC not in scope

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The only availability incident in the period was a 20-minute degradation resolved via a Slack thread with timestamped detection and resolution messages; there is no formal incident-ticketing system.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Process-exists attributes pass on the substance of response and resolution being documented, not on the formality of the tracking tool. The Slack thread contains the required detection and resolution timestamps.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include records showing availability incidents were responded to and resolved?

attributes.text: System availability status is communicated to customers through a status page or equivalent channel
attributes.typical_evidence: Public status page or equivalent customer facing channel showing current system availability
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: A customer facing channel exists that the entity uses to communicate availability status and outages, such as a public status page, and it reflects live system status. FAIL: No customer facing channel exists for communicating availability, or customers are given no availability notice during outages. NOTE: A channel that shows historical incident posts for past outages strengthens this; a live channel that has not yet had a real outage to report still passes on existence.
attributes.na_condition: N/A if Availability TSC not in scope

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The company communicates outage updates to customers through a dedicated Slack Connect channel rather than a public status.io-style page.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: any customer-facing channel the entity actually uses to communicate availability satisfies this attribute, not specifically a branded status page. The Slack Connect channel is a live equivalent.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The marketing homepage displays a static '99.9% uptime' badge, and this was accepted as the customer-facing availability communication channel.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A marketing claim is not a live status communication channel. The attribute requires an actual channel that reflects current system status and can carry outage notices, not a static badge.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a customer facing channel that communicates system availability status?

attributes.text: A threshold or set of criteria defines which incidents require a post-incident review
attributes.typical_evidence: Incident response documentation or policy stating the severity or criteria that triggers a post-incident review
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Incident response documentation defines the threshold or criteria, such as a severity level or customer impact, that triggers a post-incident review. FAIL: No defined criteria for when a post-incident review is required. NOTE: The criteria may be simple, such as any incident at or above a stated severity, but it must be written down rather than left to memory.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: There is no standalone post-incident-review policy, but the IR plan has a labeled line stating that any incident causing customer-facing downtime or data exposure gets a written review, with everything below that handled informally.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: the attribute requires the review criteria to exist in writing, not to live in a separately titled standalone document. The IR plan states a concrete impact-and-severity threshold that triggers a review, which is exactly what the attribute tests.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The incident response plan devotes two pages to post-incident reviews: a template, required attendees, and a five-business-day target for holding the session. Nowhere does it state which incidents require one. The security lead said in the walkthrough that they run a review 'whenever something affects customers.'
calibration_examples.reasoning: The trigger has to be written down, because a threshold left in someone's memory cannot be applied consistently or tested later. A well-specified review process with no stated threshold means nothing determines when a review is owed, and a verbal rule of thumb from one person is exactly what this attribute asks the entity to reduce to writing.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include documented criteria for which incidents require a post-incident review?

attributes.text: For incidents that meet the review threshold, a written post-incident review documents what happened, the impact, and corrective actions
attributes.typical_evidence: Post-incident review documents capturing the incident summary, impact, and corrective actions
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if for the incidents that crossed the review threshold a written post-incident review exists that captures what happened, the impact, and the corrective actions; if no incidents crossed the threshold during the period, pass by default on the defined process. FAIL if a qualifying incident occurred with no written review, or a review omits what happened, impact, or corrective actions. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every qualifying incident in the period has a written review covering what happened, impact, and corrective actions; isolated misses in an otherwise working practice are an exception, not a gap; systematic absence is a gap. FAIL if qualifying incidents routinely lack a written review.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The defined threshold is any incident causing customer-facing downtime. During the period the only event was a two-minute internal staging glitch that never reached customers, so nothing crossed the threshold, and no post-incident review was written.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Apply the pass-by-default clause when it is written into the pass criteria: if no incident crossed the review threshold, the attribute passes on the defined process. The one event fell below the stated threshold, so the absence of a written review is expected rather than a gap.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a written post-incident review capturing what happened, impact, and corrective actions?

attributes.text: Corrective actions from post-incident reviews are tracked through to completion
attributes.typical_evidence: Issue tracker records showing corrective action items linked to incidents, with completion status and dates
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if corrective actions from reviews are recorded in a tracker with an owner and status, and completed actions show a completion date; if no corrective actions were open during the period, pass by default on the tracking practice. FAIL if corrective actions are named but tracked nowhere. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every corrective action in the period was tracked and reached a completed state, or remain open within a reasonable timeframe with evidence of follow-up; isolated misses in an otherwise working practice are an exception, not a gap; systematic absence is a gap. FAIL if corrective actions are routinely left untracked or open indefinitely with no follow-up.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Corrective actions from the one post-incident review are logged as GitHub issues with an assignee and a status label, and the closed ones show a completion date, rather than sitting in a dedicated 'corrective action tracker' spreadsheet.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A tracking attribute passes on any system that records the action with an owner and status, not only a purpose-built corrective-action log. GitHub issues with an assignee, status label, and completion dates satisfy the owner-and-status tracking the attribute requires.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include corrective actions tracked to completion with status and dates?

attributes.text: A documented rule governs whether and how production or customer data may be used in development and test environments
attributes.typical_evidence: Data handling policy or standard stating whether production data is prohibited in non-production, or permitted only when masked and approved
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: A written rule states whether production or customer data may be used in development and test environments, and where it is permitted, requires masking or anonymization and named approval. FAIL: No documented rule, or the rule does not address production or customer data in non-production environments.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A section of the company's broader Data Classification and Acceptable Use policy states that production and customer data must never be copied into development or test environments; there is no standalone 'non-production data' document.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A documented rule can live inside a broader policy rather than in a dedicated standalone document. A written clause clearly prohibiting production and customer data in non-production environments is exactly the rule this attribute requires, so demanding a separate document is over-literal.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a written rule covering the use of production or customer data in development and test environments?

attributes.text: Non-production environments are populated with synthetic, masked, or sampled data rather than raw production data
attributes.typical_evidence: Seed or data-generation scripts producing synthetic records, or a masking configuration applied to any imported data
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Configuration or scripts show non-production environments are populated with synthetic, fabricated, masked, or sampled data. No raw production database dump is restored directly into a non-production environment. FAIL: A non-production environment is populated from a raw production copy with no masking, or no seeding or masking mechanism exists.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The seed script for the staging environment uses a fake-data library to generate all customer records; there is no separate artifact labeled 'masking configuration.'
calibration_examples.reasoning: A seed script that generates synthetic records IS the seeding mechanism this attribute asks for, even though nothing is labeled 'masking config.' The substance, fully synthetic non-production data rather than a raw production copy, is what the criteria require, not the artifact's name.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A staging database was restored from a production snapshot last month; an engineer says in the interview that they 'usually scrub PII after restoring' but no masking script or config was found in the repository or infrastructure.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. Without an actual masking script, job, or config to inspect, a raw production restore backed only by a spoken claim of scrubbing is a raw production copy with no verifiable masking, which fails this attribute.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration or seed scripts show that non-production environments use synthetic, masked, or sampled data rather than raw production data?

attributes.text: Over the examination period, production or customer data reaching a non-production environment is masked or approved in line with the rule, or the entity attests no such copying occurred
attributes.typical_evidence: Attestation of no-copy practice, or for any permitted copy, evidence of the masking step and the approval recorded
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if the entity shows either a no-copy practice consistent with the rule, or that any current non-production data set was masked or approved as the rule requires. FAIL if raw production data sits in a non-production environment contrary to the rule. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every instance of production data entering a non-production environment in the period was masked or approved per the rule, or the entity attests and evidence supports that no copying occurred; isolated misses in an otherwise working practice are an exception, not a gap; systematic absence is a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The company runs a single environment with no separate staging or development database; an architecture diagram and infrastructure inventory confirm only one environment exists, so the entity attests no production data has ever been copied anywhere.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A corroborated no-copy attestation is a legitimate pass path for this attribute at the design stage. When an architecture diagram and inventory show no non-production environment exists at all, an attestation of no copying is fully consistent with the evidence and should pass, not be gapped for lacking masking proof that could never apply.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The client attests that production data is never copied into development or test environments. The environment setup script submitted for the change control walkthrough restores the previous night's production database snapshot into the staging instance, with no masking step, and its scheduler entry runs daily.
calibration_examples.reasoning: An attestation of no copying is only available where nothing in the record contradicts it, and here the entity's own automation performs the copy nightly. Raw production data landing in a non-production environment on a schedule is the exact condition this attribute fails, whatever the intent stated elsewhere.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show that any production data used in non-production was masked or approved per the rule, or that no such copying occurred?

attributes.text: An inventory of third-party applications and integrations granted OAuth or API access to core systems is maintained
attributes.typical_evidence: System-generated list of connected apps and integrations per core system (code repository, workspace, messaging) with granted scopes
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: An inventory lists the third-party apps and integrations with OAuth or API access to core systems, and it reconciles with what those systems report as connected. FAIL: No inventory of connected integrations, or the inventory omits apps the systems report as installed.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A live screenshot of GitHub's 'Installed GitHub Apps' page covers all repository integrations, and a separate live screenshot of Slack's connected-apps page was submitted elsewhere in the evidence set rather than combined into one file.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verify the corpus before failing: live system captures are valid inventory evidence regardless of which file or folder they were submitted in. Check across the full evidence set for both systems before concluding the inventory is incomplete.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The evidence cited is the identity provider vendor's public marketing page describing that it 'integrates securely with third-party apps,' with no actual list of this organization's connected integrations.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A provider's marketing page is not this organization's configuration. The attribute requires this entity's own inventory of connected apps that reconciles with what its systems report, not a general description of the vendor's capability.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system output show the third-party apps and integrations connected to core systems with their granted scopes?

attributes.text: Third-party integrations are granted only the access scopes they need to function
attributes.typical_evidence: Per-integration scope or permission listing from each core system showing the access each app holds
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: The granted scopes for each connected integration correspond to its stated purpose, with no integration holding broad administrative access it does not need. FAIL: One or more integrations hold organization-wide or administrative scopes with no purpose justifying that access.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A CI/CD integration holds a repo:admin scope in GitHub, which its setup documentation shows is required for it to manage branch protection rules as part of its stated function.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: an administrative-sounding scope is not automatically excessive when the integration's documented purpose actually requires that level of access. Confirm the scope against the stated function before flagging it as over-privileged.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A client-authored document states 'all third-party integrations have been reviewed and are appropriately scoped,' with no export from GitHub or Slack showing the actual granted scopes per integration.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A client-authored assertion is not system proof for a configuration claim. The actual granted scopes per integration must be shown from the systems themselves, not summarized in a self-made statement.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that each integration's granted scopes match its purpose rather than broad unused access?

attributes.text: Connected integrations are reviewed on a defined cadence and unused or over-scoped integrations are removed
attributes.typical_evidence: Review records with dates, and evidence of integrations removed or scopes reduced following a review
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if a review of connected integrations has been performed and its result is recorded, including any removals or scope reductions. FAIL if no review has occurred or none is recorded. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if all scheduled reviews in the period occurred and unused or over-scoped integrations identified were removed or reduced; isolated misses in an otherwise working practice are an exception, not a gap; systematic absence is a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A solo founder logs integration reviews as dated entries in a personal task app, including a note that one unused analytics integration was disconnected after the most recent check.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Judge against the minimum acceptable design for a very small company: an informal but dated, documented review that records an actual removal is a proportional pass, not a requirement for a formal review committee or ticketing process.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Submitted as the integration review: a one page document the client wrote titled 'OAuth app review, completed', stating that all connected integrations were reviewed and found appropriate. It names no integrations, carries no date beyond the file's creation, and no export or screenshot of the connected applications page was provided.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A recorded review has to show what was reviewed and what came of it, because a conclusion with no population behind it cannot be re-performed or tested. A self-written statement that everything was found appropriate is the assertion this attribute asks the entity to support, not support for it.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a record that connected integrations were reviewed on the defined cadence?
Does the evidence show that unused or over-scoped integrations were removed or their scopes reduced?

attributes.text: Automated dependency update or security alerting is enabled for production repositories
attributes.typical_evidence: Dependency tooling configuration (Dependabot, Renovate, or equivalent) showing alerting enabled across production repositories
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Configuration shows automated dependency update or security alerting enabled for the production repositories, covering the languages and package ecosystems in use. FAIL: Alerting is not enabled, or production repositories are excluded from coverage.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A screenshot of the GitHub organization's security settings shows Dependabot alerts and security updates enabled as an org-wide default applying to all repositories, rather than a separate per-repository screenshot for each production repo.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: an org-wide default configuration that necessarily covers every production repository satisfies coverage without requiring a repeated per-repo capture.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An engineering wiki page states 'Dependabot is enabled on all our repos,' but no screenshot or export of the actual GitHub security settings was provided.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A client-authored statement is not system proof for a configuration claim; it needs a capture of the platform's own settings or corroboration against a live view. The wiki claim alone does not verify the setting is actually enabled.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show automated dependency alerting enabled across production repositories?

attributes.text: The entity defines a window for remediating vulnerable dependencies by severity
attributes.typical_evidence: Policy or standard stating remediation timelines for critical, high, and lower severity dependency advisories
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: A written window defines how quickly vulnerable dependencies are addressed, differentiated by severity. FAIL: No defined remediation window, or the window does not vary by severity.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An internal engineering handbook page (actively maintained, referenced in onboarding, not marked draft) sets remediation windows of 7 days for critical, 30 for high, and 90 for medium/low dependency advisories, but it is not labeled a formal 'security policy.'
calibration_examples.reasoning: Judge the substance of an adopted, in-use document rather than its title; a handbook page that is actually followed and defines severity-differentiated windows satisfies the attribute even without a formal policy label.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The engineering handbook's dependency section reads: 'Vulnerable dependencies are patched promptly, with critical issues prioritized ahead of routine upgrades.' No number of days appears anywhere, and no separate expectation is stated for any severity level.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A window is a stated period, so promptly is a posture rather than the window this attribute requires. Prioritising critical work is also not the same as differentiating the window by severity, and with no number written down nothing can later be found late.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a documented remediation window for dependency vulnerabilities by severity?

attributes.text: For each dependency advisory, the vulnerability was addressed within the entity's defined window
attributes.typical_evidence: Resolved dependency alerts or update pull requests showing the opened date and the fixed date for critical and high advisories
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if resolved dependency advisories show fixes applied within the entity's window, and no critical or high advisory is open beyond it. FAIL if critical or high advisories sit open past the window with no remediation. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every critical and high advisory in the period was remediated within the defined window, or upgraded and closed with a documented reason; isolated misses in an otherwise working practice are an exception, not a gap; systematic absence is a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Resolved Dependabot pull requests reference the CVE ID in the title and show the alert-opened date and merge date, but there is no separately labeled 'advisory record' document tying the two together.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verify the corpus before failing; the pull request itself, showing opened and fixed dates against a named CVE, is the underlying record the attribute asks for and should be judged on its content, not on the absence of a separately formatted advisory log.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include actual resolved dependency alerts or pull requests showing opened and fixed dates (not just a verbal description)?
Does the record show that critical and high advisories were addressed within the entity's defined window?

attributes.text: A maintained inventory of SaaS applications and tools in use is kept with an owner and update dates
attributes.typical_evidence: SaaS or tool inventory (spreadsheet, Notion database, or equivalent) listing each tool with an owner and carrying recent update or review dates
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: An inventory lists the SaaS applications and tools in use, assigns an owner, and carries dates showing it is maintained within the last twelve months. FAIL: No inventory, or a list with no owner and no evidence of maintenance.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The SaaS inventory is maintained live inside a SaaS-management platform dashboard (showing owner assignments and a last-synced timestamp for each entry) rather than a manually dated spreadsheet.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A live system's own maintenance timestamp is direct evidence the inventory is kept current, insisting on a manually entered 'update date' column when the platform's native last-synced field already proves recency is over-literalism.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a SaaS and tool inventory with an owner and recent update dates?

attributes.text: Each inventory entry identifies the sensitivity or type of data the tool holds, including which tools hold customer data
attributes.typical_evidence: Inventory entries showing a data-sensitivity or data-type field, flagging tools that hold customer or confidential data
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: The inventory records for each tool the sensitivity or type of data it holds and clearly identifies the tools that hold customer or confidential data. FAIL: The inventory does not indicate data sensitivity, or does not identify which tools hold customer data.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The inventory has a 'Data Type' column, but it is populated for only a handful of tools flagged as 'important,' while most rows, including several tools that plausibly touch customer data, are left blank or marked 'N/A.'
calibration_examples.reasoning: Partial population of a data-sensitivity field for a few tools does not satisfy a requirement that the inventory identify sensitivity for its entries generally, especially which tools hold customer data. Crediting a mostly-blank column because a few rows are filled over-credits a weak artifact.

coverage_checks.question: Does the inventory show the data sensitivity or data type held by each tool, including which hold customer data?

attributes.text: The inventory is reviewed on a defined cadence and new tools are added as they are adopted
attributes.typical_evidence: Review or update records with dates, and inventory entries for recently adopted tools
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if the inventory shows a recent review and includes tools adopted recently, indicating it is kept current. FAIL if the inventory is stale or omits tools known to be in use. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if the scheduled reviews in the period occurred and newly adopted tools were added to the inventory; isolated misses in an otherwise working practice are an exception, not a gap; systematic absence is a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A quarterly SaaS inventory review was completed six weeks ago (recorded as a dated changelog entry), and two tools adopted in the last two months already appear as rows; the evaluator fails it because there is no separate signed 'review sign-off' form.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A process-exists attribute at the design stage passes on evidence the inventory is kept current, not on a specific sign-off artifact, a recent dated review plus recently-adopted tools already captured demonstrates the cadence is real and working. Demanding a formal sign-off form when the changelog and up-to-date rows already prove currency manufactures a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The SaaS inventory carries a review note dated two months ago and an owner for each of its 14 entries. The identity provider's connected applications list and the card statement submitted for vendor testing both show three tools in active use that the inventory does not contain: a design tool, a note taking app, and an AI transcription service.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A review is judged by whether the inventory came out of it current, not by whether a review was recorded. The criteria fail an inventory that omits tools known to be in use, and tools adopted directly by a team are exactly the ones a review has to catch, since they are the ones no procurement step ever saw.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show the inventory was reviewed on the defined cadence and updated with newly adopted tools?

attributes.text: Retention periods are defined for the classes of customer data
attributes.typical_evidence: Data retention policy or schedule stating how long each class of customer data is kept
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: A retention schedule defines how long each class of customer data is retained. FAIL: No defined retention periods, or the schedule does not cover the customer data the entity holds. NOTE: These periods are the benchmark against which the automated expiry and executed deletion tested elsewhere in this control are measured. Where a retention schedule is already maintained, the periods it sets for customer data classes satisfy this attribute.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Retention periods for customer data classes are defined in the same schedule already reviewed and passed under the data retention control; no separate DAT-05-specific document was submitted.
calibration_examples.reasoning: The attribute's own note states that where a retention schedule is already maintained, the periods it sets for customer data classes satisfy this attribute. Demanding a duplicate standalone document double-counts the same requirement, so this passes on the existing schedule.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include defined retention periods for the classes of customer data?

attributes.text: Backups and stored data age out per a configured lifecycle rather than being retained indefinitely
attributes.typical_evidence: Storage lifecycle rules and backup retention settings showing automatic expiration
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Configuration shows backups and stored data expire automatically per a set retention window aligned to the retention schedule. FAIL: Backups or storage are configured with no expiration or indefinite retention contrary to the schedule.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An AWS console export shows an S3 lifecycle rule expiring objects after 90 days, matching the documented retention schedule, but the export itself carries no label tying it explicitly to 'the retention schedule.'
calibration_examples.reasoning: A live system export showing an expiration window that numerically matches the documented schedule is sufficient proof of alignment. An explicit cross-reference annotation inside the export is not required when the configured window plainly matches the benchmark.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A client-authored spreadsheet lists S3 buckets alongside a 'retention: 90 days' column, but no AWS console screenshot, CLI output, or API export of the actual lifecycle configuration was provided.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof. A configuration claim about live infrastructure needs an actual system capture or corroboration, not a spreadsheet the company typed itself, so this gaps pending a real export.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show backups and stored data age out on a set retention window?

attributes.text: For an executed deletion, the customer data was removed within the entity's defined window
attributes.typical_evidence: Deletion record or system evidence showing a customer's data removed following account deletion or a deletion request
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if a deletion example shows the customer's associated data removed and the account no longer present, consistent with the retention schedule. FAIL if data persists after deletion beyond the defined window. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every deletion in the period removed the associated customer data within the defined window; isolated misses in an otherwise working practice are an exception, not a gap; systematic absence is a gap.
attributes.na_condition: Pass if no customer data deletions were requested or required during the period

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: One customer deletion occurred this period; an automated job log shows the deletion job completed on a given date, and a support ticket in a separate system shows the original request date, with the two together falling within the defined retention window.
calibration_examples.reasoning: The requirement is that the evidence corpus as a whole shows removal within the window, not that one single record contain every fact. A job completion log plus a corroborating support ticket together plainly establish timely deletion, which satisfies the design-stage pass.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual deletion record or system output showing customer data removed (not just a verbal description)?
Does the record show that the data was removed within the entity's defined window?

attributes.text: A current list of subprocessors is maintained and made available to customers
attributes.typical_evidence: Published subprocessor list (public page or customer-accessible document) naming each subprocessor and the data it processes
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: A subprocessor list is published or made available to customers and reflects the vendors currently processing customer data. FAIL: No subprocessor list, or a list that is stale or omits vendors known to process customer data.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The public subprocessors page is live and lists every vendor matching the internal vendor inventory, but the page has no visible 'last updated' date, and the AI treated the absence of a date stamp as evidence the list is stale.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: what matters is whether the published list substantively matches the vendors currently processing customer data, not whether a date stamp is displayed. Reconciliation against the internal inventory confirms it is current.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The published subprocessor page lists seven vendors and carries a recent 'last updated' date. The vendor register and the AI provider inventory each show two further processors handling customer data, a transcription API and a new email delivery service added four months ago, neither of which appears on the page.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A subprocessor list is measured against the vendors actually processing customer data, not against how recently the page was touched. The criteria fail a list that omits known processors, and the omissions here are the two most recent additions, which is the pattern a stale list always takes.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a current subprocessor list made available to customers?

attributes.text: Adding a new subprocessor follows a review step before it handles customer data
attributes.typical_evidence: Review record for a recently added subprocessor showing assessment before onboarding
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if the process requires a review before a new subprocessor handles customer data and a recent addition shows that review occurred. FAIL if subprocessors are added with no review step. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if all subprocessors added during the period were reviewed before handling customer data; isolated misses in an otherwise working practice are an exception, not a gap; systematic absence is a gap.
attributes.na_condition: Pass if no new subprocessors were added during the period

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Before a new subprocessor was enabled, the security lead approved it in a Slack thread referencing the vendor's security posture, rather than through a formal ticketing system review.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Process-exists attributes pass on the existence and use of the review step, not on the formality of the tooling used to record it. The Slack thread documents an actual pre-onboarding review by a responsible person.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show a review was performed before a new subprocessor handled customer data?

attributes.text: Customers are notified of subprocessor changes in line with the entity's commitments
attributes.typical_evidence: Customer notification, changelog entry, or subscription mechanism showing subprocessor changes are communicated
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if a mechanism notifies customers of subprocessor changes as the entity commits, and a recent change shows notice was given. FAIL if changes occur with no customer notification despite a commitment to notify. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if all subprocessor changes during the period were communicated to customers per the commitments; isolated misses in an otherwise working practice are an exception, not a gap; systematic absence is a gap.
attributes.na_condition: Pass if the entity makes no commitment to notify customers of subprocessor changes and no changes occurred during the period

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The team states that customers were emailed when a new subprocessor was added, but no copy of the notification email, changelog entry, or send log was pulled as evidence.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never adequate evidence of an actual notification event. The attribute requires a record of the notice itself, such as the sent email or changelog entry, not a claim that it was sent.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show customers were notified of subprocessor changes per the commitments?

attributes.text: Automated outage and error alerts are configured to reach the founder on a channel they actively monitor, and delivery has been confirmed
attributes.typical_evidence: Alert or monitor configuration from the error tracking or monitoring tool showing an outage or error rule with the founder as the notification target, plus a screenshot of a received alert or successful test notification
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Alert configuration from the monitoring or error tracking tool shows at least one active rule for outages or errors whose notification target is a channel the founder actually monitors, such as personal email, phone, SMS, or a direct message, and a received alert or successful test notification confirms delivery reached the founder. FAIL: No outage or error alert rule exists, alerts route only to an inbox or channel the founder does not monitor, or delivery cannot be confirmed.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The monitoring tool's alert rule routes outage notifications to a Slack DM the founder checks constantly on their phone rather than to email, and a test alert fired last week was received there.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Judge the attribute's actual requirement, which is a channel the founder actively monitors, not a specific channel type like email. A Slack DM the founder checks constantly, with a received test alert confirming delivery, satisfies both required elements.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A screenshot shows an alert rule pointing to a shared team support inbox that is checked sporadically, and no test notification or received alert was provided to confirm delivery.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A configuration screenshot alone is not proof the founder actually receives the alert. The target is not a channel the founder actively monitors and delivery was never confirmed, so the attribute fails on both required elements.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include the alert configuration showing an outage or error rule with the founder as the notification target?
Does the evidence include a received alert or successful test notification confirming delivery reached the founder?

attributes.text: The founder is subscribed to outage or status notifications for the critical third party providers the product depends on
attributes.typical_evidence: Screenshots or confirmation emails of status page or outage subscriptions for the hosting, database, authentication, and payment providers the product relies on
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Evidence shows the founder is subscribed to outage or status notifications for the critical third party providers the product depends on, covering categories such as hosting, database, authentication, and payment processing, so provider incidents are learned promptly. FAIL: No provider status subscriptions exist for any critical dependency, or subscriptions cover none of the providers the product actually runs on.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The founder uses a single status-monitoring integration that watches the hosting, database, authentication, and payment providers' status pages and pushes any change to their phone, but there are no separate per-provider subscription confirmation emails.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Judge whether the founder is actually notified of provider outages, not whether each subscription took a specific enrollment form. A monitoring integration covering all four critical categories and delivering to the founder's phone is a subscription to outage notifications in substance, so it passes.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Screenshots of the founder's email inbox show confirmation messages for hosting and database provider status subscriptions, but the evidence for the authentication and payment providers is only a screenshot of each provider's public status page, never visited from a logged-in subscribed account.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A provider's public status or marketing page is not proof of this org's own subscription. Viewing a status page is not the same as being enrolled to receive its notifications, so two of the four required provider categories remain unsubstantiated.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show subscriptions to outage or status notifications for the critical third party providers the product depends on?

attributes.text: A lightweight incident log and a ready customer communication template are maintained
attributes.typical_evidence: A simple incident log (spreadsheet, Notion page, or issue tracker view) with at least one entry or a tabletop entry, together with a drafted customer notification template
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: A lightweight incident log is maintained with a structure to record an event, its date, impact, and resolution, evidenced by at least one entry or a tabletop entry, and a customer communication template is drafted and ready to send if an incident affects customers. FAIL: No incident log exists in any form, or no customer communication template is prepared.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The incident log lives as a Notion database view titled 'Incidents' with one real entry recording date, impact, and resolution, plus a saved customer email draft ready to send.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: the attribute requires a lightweight log and a ready template in any reasonable form, not specifically a spreadsheet. A Notion database entry with the required fields, plus a drafted template, satisfies both elements.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A lightweight incident log is maintained and genuinely used: three entries with dates, impact, and resolution, including one real booking outage. No customer communication template exists in any form; the founder said they would write something at the time if it were ever needed.
calibration_examples.reasoning: This attribute names two artifacts and a strong showing on one does not carry the other, however lightweight the control is meant to be. The template exists to be ready before the incident, so an intention to draft one under pressure is the absence the attribute is testing for.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a lightweight incident log with at least one entry or a tabletop entry?
Does the evidence include a drafted customer communication template ready to send?

attributes.text: For any incident in the period, post incident notes record the root cause and a follow up action
attributes.typical_evidence: Post incident notes or a tabletop note capturing what happened, the root cause, and a follow up action, drawn from the incident log or issue tracker
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if the entity can show at least one post incident note or tabletop note capturing what happened, the root cause, and a follow up action, demonstrating the practice exists. FAIL if no post incident notes and no tabletop note exist. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every incident in the period has a post incident note recording the root cause and a follow up action; isolated misses in an otherwise working practice are an exception, not a gap; systematic absence is a gap. NOTE: if no incidents occurred during the period, a tabletop or dry run note serves as the evaluation basis.
attributes.na_condition: Pass basis shifts to a tabletop or dry run note if no incidents occurred during the period

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: No incidents occurred during the period. The team ran a dry-run of their process and wrote a short shared doc titled 'Incident Simulation Notes' naming a plausible root cause and one follow-up action.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Process-exists attributes pass on the existence and use of the practice, and the pass criteria explicitly allow a tabletop or dry-run note as the evaluation basis when no incidents occurred. The simulation note captures root cause and a follow-up action as required.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual post incident note or tabletop note recording the root cause and a follow up action (not just a verbal description)?

attributes.text: Counterparties that create, receive, maintain, or transmit ePHI are identified
attributes.typical_evidence: Vendor or customer inventory with an ePHI flag, or a data flow document naming ePHI counterparties
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: An inventory or data flow document identifies which customers and subcontractors handle ePHI, and it is consistent with the vendor inventory. FAIL: No identification of ePHI-handling counterparties, or the list contradicts the vendor inventory.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The vendor register has an ePHI column and the data flow document names the same three counterparties (cloud provider, transcription API, EHR integration partner). No separate HIPAA-titled inventory exists.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Judge substance over form: an ePHI flag on the existing vendor register plus a consistent data flow document is the identification this attribute asks for. A separately titled HIPAA inventory is not required.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The data flow diagram shows ePHI flowing to an analytics vendor, but the vendor register's ePHI column marks only the cloud provider.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A contradiction between the identification and the flow evidence fails the attribute. The inventory must agree with where ePHI actually goes, and an unflagged recipient is exactly the counterparty most likely to be missing a BAA.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an inventory or data flow document identifying which customers and subcontractors handle ePHI?

attributes.text: For each customer relationship involving ePHI: a signed BAA is in place
attributes.typical_evidence: Executed BAA documents with signature dates
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Each ePHI customer relationship has a BAA signed on or before the date ePHI handling began. FAIL: Any relationship lacks a signed BAA, or the BAA postdates the start of ePHI handling with no documented interim arrangement.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Three customers each have an executed BAA. One was signed two weeks after the pilot began but states an effective date of the pilot start, and the executed pilot agreement already bound both parties to Security Rule compliance, subcontractor flow-down, and security incident reporting for that window.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A documented interim arrangement qualifies when the required terms actually covered the entire handling window; here the pilot agreement carried the BAA content and the executed BAA is effective from day one. Failing this on signature order alone is over-literal.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The client states every customer signs a BAA at onboarding and shows the onboarding checklist template containing a BAA step, but no executed agreement is produced for any customer.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A population-tested attribute needs the executed artifact for the items tested. A process description or checklist template never substitutes for the signed document.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: One BAA was signed three months after ePHI handling began. The client offers a dated email in which the customer agreed to keep pilot data confidential; the email contains no security obligations and no retroactive effect.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A documented interim arrangement must carry the required agreement content for the exposure window. A generic confidentiality email with no security terms and no retroactive effect does not, so the late signature stands uncured.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include executed customer BAAs with signature dates for the ePHI customer relationships (not just a template or a process description)?

attributes.text: For each subcontractor that handles ePHI: a signed downstream BAA is in place
attributes.typical_evidence: Executed subcontractor BAAs, including cloud provider BAA (for example the AWS, GCP, or Azure BAA)
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Each ePHI-handling subcontractor, including the cloud infrastructure provider, has a signed BAA. FAIL: Any ePHI-handling subcontractor operates without a BAA. Note: a subcontractor that only transmits ePHI transiently and never stores it, or a service that receives no ePHI at all, may be excluded only with a documented rationale. A vendor that stores or maintains ePHI remains a business associate even when the data is encrypted and the vendor holds no decryption key.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The AWS BAA was accepted through AWS Artifact and the client shows the Artifact acceptance page with the account id and acceptance date. No countersigned PDF exists.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Console acceptance through the provider's agreement mechanism is the standard executed form of a cloud BAA. Requiring a wet-signature PDF is over-literal.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An error-monitoring vendor receives stack traces that can include patient names. The client excluded it from BAA scope with a note reading 'logs only'.
calibration_examples.reasoning: An exclusion rationale must establish that the subcontractor cannot access ePHI. 'Logs only' does not establish that when the logs carry patient data, so the exclusion fails and the vendor needs a BAA.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An offsite backup vendor stores encrypted database snapshots containing ePHI. The client excluded it from BAA scope with the rationale that the client holds the encryption keys and the vendor only ever sees ciphertext.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A vendor that stores or maintains ePHI is a business associate even when the data is encrypted and the vendor holds no key. The ciphertext rationale does not remove the BAA requirement; only transient transmission or receiving no ePHI at all can.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include executed BAAs for the ePHI-handling subcontractors, including the cloud infrastructure provider?

attributes.text: BAA terms include the elements required by 45 CFR 164.314(a)(2)
attributes.typical_evidence: The BAA template or executed agreements
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Terms require Security Rule compliance, flow-down of the same obligations to subcontractors, and upstream reporting of security incidents including breaches. FAIL: Any of the three required elements is absent from the operative BAA.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The BAA template requires Security Rule compliance and breach reporting but says nothing about subcontractors. The client notes that in practice every subcontractor signs the same template.
calibration_examples.reasoning: The flow-down obligation must appear in the operative terms. The client's practice of signing subcontractors does not put the required clause into the agreement, and the practice is invisible to the counterparty relying on it.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The executed BAA incorporates the customer's standard BAA rider by reference. The rider, provided in evidence, contains all three required elements.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Terms incorporated by reference are operative terms. Judge the assembled agreement the parties are bound by, not a single document in isolation.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include the BAA template or an executed BAA showing Security Rule compliance, subcontractor flow-down, and incident reporting terms?

attributes.text: Emergency access procedure is documented, covering when it applies and who may invoke it
attributes.typical_evidence: Break-glass or emergency access section of the access control policy or runbook
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: A documented procedure defines the circumstances that qualify as an emergency, who is authorized to invoke emergency access, and the steps to obtain it. FAIL: No documented emergency access procedure, or the procedure names no authorized personnel.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The access control policy has a break-glass section: it applies when the identity provider is down or all administrators are unreachable, either founder may invoke it, and the steps point to the vault entry holding the root credential.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A section within the access control policy satisfies the documentation requirement. A standalone emergency access document is not required when the section covers circumstances, authorized people, and steps.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The client walks through a sensible break-glass process in conversation and shows the vault entry it uses, but no written procedure exists anywhere in the policy suite or runbooks.
calibration_examples.reasoning: The attribute tests documentation. A working practice described verbally fails it, because in a real emergency the people who know the process may be exactly the ones unreachable.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a written emergency access procedure covering qualifying circumstances, authorized personnel, and steps?

attributes.text: Emergency access paths are inventoried, restricted, and secured
attributes.typical_evidence: Break-glass account list, vault entry, or root credential storage configuration
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Emergency credentials or access paths are enumerated, limited to the personnel named in the procedure, and stored securely (vault, sealed credential, or hardware token). FAIL: Emergency credentials are undocumented, broadly available, or stored in plaintext.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A dedicated vault holds the cloud root credential, the vault access report lists only the two founders named in the procedure, and the root MFA device sits in a fire safe noted in the vault entry.
calibration_examples.reasoning: The criterion accepts any secure storage form: vault, sealed credential, or hardware token. A restricted vault entry with a physically secured MFA device qualifies; a hardware token is not specifically required.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The root password sits in the shared engineering vault that all eight engineers can read. The client notes it has never been used.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Broadly available emergency credentials fail the restriction requirement. Storage in a vault does not by itself restrict access to the personnel the procedure names, and non-use does not cure over-availability.

coverage_checks.question: Does the configuration evidence show the emergency credentials enumerated, limited to the named personnel, and stored securely?

attributes.text: For each emergency access use (if any): use was logged and reviewed afterward
attributes.typical_evidence: Access logs for the break-glass identity plus the post-use review record
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Each use is logged and has a documented after-the-fact review confirming the use was appropriate. FAIL: Any use is unlogged or lacks a post-use review. If no uses occurred in the period, the attribute passes on the logging configuration being in place.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: No emergency access occurred during the period. The audit trail shows zero root sign-ins and the break-glass vault entry's access history is empty; both pulls are recorded with their commands.
calibration_examples.reasoning: With zero uses, the attribute passes on the logging configuration being in place, and the recorded empty pulls are the evidence of zero. Do not fail an empty population for lacking review records.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: One root sign-in appears in the audit trail during an identity provider outage. The incident retrospective describes the outage but never examines the emergency access session itself.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Each use needs a documented after-the-fact review of the access itself: who signed in, what was done, whether it was appropriate. An incident retro that never looks at the emergency session is not that review.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include the break-glass identity's access log for the period, and a post-use review record for any use shown?

attributes.text: A six year retention requirement is defined for security policies and security activity records
attributes.typical_evidence: Retention schedule or policy governance section naming the six year floor for security documentation
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: A documented retention requirement of at least six years covers security policies and the records of security activities (risk assessments, reviews, incidents, training). FAIL: No retention requirement for security documentation, or a period shorter than six years.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The data retention schedule covers customer data (24 months) and application logs (12 months). Security policies and the records of security activities appear nowhere in it.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Customer data retention is a different object from security documentation retention. A thorough schedule that never mentions security policies or activity records fails this attribute regardless of how well it covers everything else.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The policy governance section states that security policies and security activity records are retained for at least six years from creation or the date last in effect, whichever is later. There is no standalone retention schedule document.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A sentence in the policy governance section is a documented requirement. A dedicated retention schedule document is not required when the requirement is written, scoped to security documentation, and reaches six years.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a written retention requirement of at least six years covering security policies and security activity records?

attributes.text: Historical versions of policies and security records are retrievable
attributes.typical_evidence: Document repository version history, archive folder, or system-of-record retention configuration
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: The storage system demonstrably preserves prior versions (version history enabled, archive maintained, or deletion restricted) so a document from an earlier period can be produced. FAIL: Prior versions are overwritten or deleted with no archive.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Policies live in a shared drive with version history enabled, and the client opens a prior version of the security policy from 14 months ago on screen.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Version history that actually produces an earlier version demonstrates retrievability. A separate formal archive system is not required when the repository preserves and serves prior versions.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Policies are edited in place in a workspace tool whose plan limits page history to the last 7 days. The client intends to upgrade the plan.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Retrievability must actually reach back to earlier periods. A 7 day history window cannot produce prior versions, and an intention to upgrade is not a configuration.

coverage_checks.question: Does the configuration evidence show prior versions preserved and retrievable (version history, archive, or restricted deletion)?
